- ❌ "`-fno-elide-constructors` turns off all elision." ✅ In C++17 and later it cannot turn off guaranteed prvalue elision.

edge_cases.title: Deleted move constructor does not fall back to copy
Non-movable types: prvalue yes, named local no
edge_cases.explanation:
- With `NM(const NM&) = delete; NM(NM&&) = delete;`:
  - `NM make() { return NM{1}; }` compiles in C++17 (error in C++14).
  - `NM make() { NM x{1}; return x; }` never compiles, even though the compiler would apply NRVO: the move/copy constructor must be usable for the non-guaranteed case.
  - `NM n = cond ? NM{1} : NM{2};` compiles: both branches are prvalues.
  - `n = make();` fails: assignment needs `operator=`, elision does not help.

edge_cases.title: `return std::move(local)` disables NRVO
edge_cases.explanation:
- Output with a tracing type: `ctor move dtor dtor` instead of `ctor dtor`.
- GCC: `warning: moving a local object in a return statement prevents copy elision [-Wpessimizing-move]`.
- Same problem inside `return std::move(cond ? a : b);`: it moves, but a plain `if` would allow implicit move without the cast and keep code clearer.

edge_cases.title: The conditional operator copies
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T f(bool c) { T a, b; return c ? a : b; }` prints `ctor ctor copy`.
- `c ? a : b` with two lvalues of the same type is an lvalue; it is not "the name of a local", so neither NRVO nor implicit move applies.
- Fix: `if (c) return a; return b;` gives an implicit move (two candidates, so still no NRVO).

edge_cases.title: Members and structured bindings are copied
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T f() { P p; return p.first; }` copies: a member is not an implicitly movable entity.
- `T f() { auto [x, y] = P{}; return x; }` also copies when `P` is an aggregate: `x` names a member of a hidden object, not a variable of its own.
- Compiler difference: when `P` is tuple-like (`std::pair`, `std::tuple`), GCC 11 and GCC 13 in `-std=c++20` and later **move** (they treat the binding as the hidden `T&&` reference variable), while Clang 14 copies in every mode. Do not rely on either; write `std::move(x)` if a move is wanted.
- If the move is intended, write `return std::move(p.first);` and `return std::move(x);`; here `std::move` is correct, not a pessimization.

edge_cases.title: Returning a parameter moves, never elides
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T pass(T p) { return p; }` called as `pass(T{})`: the argument `T{}` is constructed directly into `p` (guaranteed), then `p` is **moved** into the result: `ctor move`.
- Writing `return std::move(p);` gives the same code but triggers `-Wredundant-move`.
- For a `T&&` parameter: `T f(T&& x) { return x; }` **copies** in C++17 and **moves** in C++20 (P1825). Clang 14 already moves in C++17 mode (it applies P1825 to older modes); GCC 11 follows the `-std` flag.

edge_cases.title: C++23 changes what `return x;` means for references
edge_cases.explanation:
- C++23 (P2266) makes a returned implicitly movable name an xvalue.
- Now valid: `T&& forward_it(T&& x) { return x; }`.
- Now invalid: `int& h(int&& x) { return x; }` (non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to an xvalue). It compiled in C++20.
- `decltype(auto)` also changes: `decltype(auto) f() { T x; return (x); }` deduces `T&` in C++20 and `T&&` in C++23 (verified with Clang 14). Both are references to a dead local: the parentheses are the bug in either standard.

edge_cases.title: Elision changes observable output (and that is legal)
edge_cases.explanation:
- A copy constructor that counts calls or logs can be skipped; code that depends on the count of copy/move constructor calls is not portable across NRVO and non-NRVO builds.
- Never put essential side effects (registration, reference counting) only in copy/move constructors.
- Destructor calls match constructor calls in every case; only the *number* of objects changes.

code_examples.title: Factories for non-movable types (C++17)
code_examples.explanation:

interview_qa.question: What is copy elision, and what is the difference between RVO and NRVO?
interview_qa.answer: Copy elision means an object is constructed directly in its final location, so a copy or move constructor that the code seems to need is never called. RVO is elision for an unnamed prvalue (`return T(args);`), guaranteed since C++17; NRVO is elision for a named local (`T t; return t;`), which is permitted but never required.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Mechanically, the caller passes the address of the result slot; the callee constructs the return value there.
- RVO in C++17 is not even an optimization any more: a prvalue has no temporary, it directly initializes its result object.
- NRVO needs the compiler to place the local at the result address from the start, which is only possible if it is the only candidate.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Both are guaranteed in C++17." Only the prvalue case is.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: elision is allowed to change observable behaviour (skipped constructors with side effects); together with allocation elision it is one of the very few exceptions to the as-if rule.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: RVO (prvalue) is guaranteed, NRVO (named) is optional.

interview_qa.question: How did implicit move on return change in C++11, C++14, C++20 and C++23?
interview_qa.answer: C++11 introduced it for returned locals and by-value parameters (try as rvalue, then as lvalue). C++14 (CWG 1579) allowed a different return type with a converting constructor. interview_qa.explanation:

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: compilers applied CWG 1579 retroactively, so in practice C++11 mode already behaves like C++14 on modern GCC/Clang.

interview_qa.question: You pass a `std::string` to a constructor that stores it. `const std::string&`, `std::string&&`, or by value?

interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
For a parameter that is always stored, take it by value and move it into the member (the sink idiom). It costs one extra move compared with a `const&`/`&&` overload pair, but gives one function that is optimal up to that move for lvalues, xvalues and prvalues.

**Explanation:**
- Measured with a tracing type: lvalue argument → `copy move`; `std::move(x)` → `move move`; prvalue → `move` (the parameter is built in place).
- Overload pair: lvalue → `copy`; rvalue → `move`. With N sink parameters you would need 2^N overloads, or a constrained forwarding template.
- Do not use by-value for read-only parameters (`const&` or `std::string_view`), or when the type is expensive to move (`std::array<double, 1000>`).
- For `std::string` specifically, a short string (SSO) "move" copies its characters, so the extra move is cheap but not free.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Always `const std::string&`, by value means a copy." For a stored parameter, `const&` forces a copy even when the caller passes a temporary.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: setters that may reuse existing capacity (`name_ = s;` into an already-large string) are a case where `const&` can beat by-value.

**Key takeaway:** Stored parameter: by value + `std::move`; read-only parameter: `const&` or a view.

interview_qa.question: Can copy elision change the output of a program?
interview_qa.answer: Yes. Copy elision is explicitly allowed to omit copy/move constructors (and the matching destructors) even when they have side effects, such as printing or counting. It is the main exception to the as-if rule.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Example: a constructor counter reads 1 move with `-fno-elide-constructors` (C++17) and 0 without it, for the same NRVO-able function.
- Destructor calls always match constructions; only the number of objects changes.
- Consequence: never put required behaviour (registration, refcount increments, logging that audit depends on) only in copy/move constructors.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Optimizations cannot change observable behaviour." True for everything else, not for elision.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: since C++14 the compiler may also elide or merge `new`/`delete` allocations (allocation elision), the other notable exception.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Elision may skip side-effecting constructors; design for it.

interview_qa.question: What does `-fno-elide-constructors` show in C++14 vs C++17?
interview_qa.answer: In C++14 it disables all elision, so `T a = rvo();` shows two moves (local → return temporary → `a`). In C++17 it can only disable NRVO: `T a = rvo();` still prints just `ctor dtor`, while `T b = nrvo();` shows one move.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured with GCC 11:
  - `-std=c++14 -fno-elide-constructors`: rvo `ctor move dtor move dtor dtor`; nrvo same.
  - `-std=c++17 -fno-elide-constructors`: rvo `ctor dtor`; nrvo `ctor move dtor dtor`.
- This is the clearest demonstration that C++17 changed the *language*, not the optimizer.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The flag turns off RVO in every standard."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: use the flag to check that a type's move constructor is correct, because NRVO normally hides it in tests.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: In C++17 the flag can only reveal the NRVO fallback.

interview_qa.question: A type registers `this` in a global registry in its constructor and removes it in its destructor. Can a factory return it by value safely?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, if the factory returns a prvalue (`return Tracked{id};`): since C++17 the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage, so the address it registered is its final address. Returning a named local is the trap: NRVO is optional, and when it does not happen a copy or move creates a second object at a different address, so the type must either fix up the registry in its copy/move constructor or delete them.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Guaranteed elision makes "construct in place, never relocate" types returnable; only prvalue returns qualify.

interview_qa.question: Does returning by value mean returning a copy in modern C++?
interview_qa.answer: No. Returning by value means the caller gets its own object; with guaranteed elision, NRVO or implicit move, building it typically costs zero or one move. It is the default for factories and for anything computed inside the function.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The usual alternative, returning a reference to a local (`const std::string& getName() { std::string n = "x"; return n; }`), is a dangling reference (see topic 01).
- Return a `const&` only to an object that outlives the call (a member, a static).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Return `const&` to avoid the copy." The referenced local is destroyed at return.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: return by value is also thread-friendly: the caller's copy cannot change under it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Return values by value; elision and move make it cheap.

interview_qa.question: Why does `v.push_back(T{})` call a move constructor while `T x = T{};` does not?
interview_qa.answer: `push_back` takes `T&&`; binding a reference to a prvalue materializes a temporary, and the vector then move-constructs its element from that temporary. Guaranteed elision does not pass through a reference parameter. `emplace_back(args)` forwards the constructor arguments and builds the element in place.
code_examples:
push_back: ctor move dtor 
emplace_back: ctor 
end: dtor dtor
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Reference parameters materialize temporaries; only `emplace` constructs in place.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
ctor 
dtor 
```
(`dtor` is printed after the newline, when `x` is destroyed at the end of `main`.)

**Explanation:**
- Every `T(...)` wrapped around a prvalue of type `T` is itself a prvalue with the same result object, so the whole chain `T(make())` → `T(T(T()))` collapses into `x`.
- One object, one constructor, one destructor; no copy or move, and it would compile even with deleted copy/move constructors.
- In C++14 (with `-fno-elide-constructors`) the same code prints a chain of moves.
- **Key Concept:** In C++17 a prvalue initializes its result object directly; nesting does not create temporaries.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::mutex` has no copy or move constructor, so `Account`'s implicit copy constructor is defined as deleted and its defaulted move constructor is deleted too.
- A defaulted move constructor that is defined as deleted is ignored by overload resolution ([class.copy.ctor]/10), so the rvalue finds the deleted copy constructor; that is why Clang names the copy constructor and GCC the move constructor.
- `open_a` returns a prvalue: guaranteed elision in C++17, no constructor needed. It compiles.
- `open_b` returns a named local: NRVO is optional, so the program must be valid without it, and there is no usable move or copy constructor.
- **Key Concept:** Non-movable types can be returned only as prvalues.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: use of deleted function 'Msg::Msg(Msg&&)' (both return statements)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The returned names are treated as rvalues. Overload resolution picks the best match for an rvalue, which is the move constructor, deleted or not. Selecting a deleted function is ill-formed; there is no second attempt with the copy constructor.
- If `Msg(Msg&&)` were simply not declared, the copy constructor would be chosen and the program would print `copy`.
- Compiler note: GCC 11 with `-std=c++17` accepts this and prints `copy`; Clang rejects it in every mode, GCC rejects it in C++20.
- **Key Concept:** A deleted move constructor is not "no move constructor": it blocks return-by-name.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
copy | copy | move 
```

**Explanation:**
- `l.price` is a member of a local, not an implicitly movable entity: copy.
- `p` is a structured binding: a name for a member of a hidden object, not a variable of its own: copy.
- `Level` is a plain aggregate here. With a tuple-like source (`std::pair`), GCC 11/13 in C++20 mode move instead, while Clang copies; do not depend on it.
- `from_param(Px{})`: the prvalue argument constructs `p` directly (no output), then the parameter is implicitly moved out. Parameters are never elided.
- Fixes for the first two: `return std::move(l.price);`, `return std::move(p);` (here `std::move` is correct, not a pessimization).
- **Key Concept:** Only whole locals and parameters named directly get implicit move.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
C++17: copy (GCC; Clang 14 prints move in every mode)
C++20: move
```

**Explanation:**
- Inside `sink`, `x` is an lvalue of type `T&&` (named rvalue reference, see topic 03).
- C++17 implicit move covered only local objects and by-value parameters, not rvalue-reference variables: copy.
- C++20 (P1825) added rvalue-reference variables to the implicitly movable entities: move. Verified with GCC 11 (`-std=c++17` vs `-std=c++20`).
- Clang 14 applies P1825 retroactively and prints `move` even with `-std=c++11`/`-std=c++17`; the C++17 `copy` is GCC's strict-mode behaviour.
- Portable code that targets both: `return std::move(x);` is correct here (it is a reference, so there is no NRVO to lose).
- **Key Concept:** Implicit move on return grew in C++20 to cover named rvalue references.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
C++20: compiles and prints 7
C++23: compile error (Clang: non-const lvalue reference to type 'int' cannot bind to a temporary of type 'int')
```

**Explanation:**
- In C++20 the id-expression `candidate` in a return statement is an lvalue when the return type is a reference, so `int&` binds to it.
- C++23 (P2266, simpler implicit move) makes the returned name of an implicitly movable entity an **xvalue** in all cases; an `int&` cannot bind to an xvalue. Verified with Clang 14: compiles with `-std=c++20`, fails with `-std=c++2b`.
- The same change makes `int&& f(int&& x) { return x; }` valid in C++23 (error before).
- Fix that works in both: `return static_cast<int&>(candidate);`, or rethink the API: returning an lvalue reference to something the caller passed as an rvalue is usually a dangling reference waiting to happen.
- **Key Concept:** C++23 changed `return name;` into an xvalue: a source-breaking change for reference returns.

quick_reference.content:
#### What happens on `return`
| Return statement | C++17/20 result |
|---|---|
| `return T(args);` | Guaranteed elision: 1 ctor |
| `return local;` (one candidate) | NRVO usually: 1 ctor; else 1 move |
| `return a;` / `return b;` on different paths | 1 move (no NRVO) |
| `return param;` | 1 move |
| `return std::move(local);` | 1 move (NRVO disabled, warning) |
| `return c ? a : b;` | 1 copy |
| `return local.member;` | 1 copy (use `std::move` if intended) |
| `return binding;` (structured binding of an aggregate) | 1 copy (GCC moves tuple-like bindings in C++20) |
| `return derived_local;` into `Base` | move + slice (C++20; copy + slice in GCC C++17 mode) |
| `return local;` into `unique_ptr<Base>` / `optional<T>` | 1 move via converting ctor |
| `T&& f(T&& x) { return x; }` | Error before C++23, OK in C++23 |
| `T f(T&& x) { return x; }` | Copy in C++17 (GCC), move in C++20 (Clang moves in all modes) |

#### Guaranteed vs permitted
| Guaranteed (C++17) | Permitted only |
|---|---|
| `T x = T(...)`, `T x = f()` (f returns prvalue) | NRVO `return local;` |
| `return T(...)` | `throw local;` / catch by value |
| By-value parameter from prvalue | |
| `new T(f())` | |
| Works with deleted copy/move | Copy/move must be accessible |

#### Warnings and flags
| Flag | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `-Wpessimizing-move` (in `-Wall`) | `return std::move(local);` |
| `-Wredundant-move` (GCC `-Wextra`) | `return std::move(param);` |
| `-fno-elide-constructors` | Disable non-mandatory elision (NRVO) to observe moves |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is RVO guaranteed? | Prvalue elision is guaranteed since C++17; NRVO is not |
| What if NRVO doesn't happen? | Implicit move; copy only if no move constructor is declared |
| Deleted move ctor on `return local;`? | Ill-formed, no fallback to copy |
| Should I `return std::move(local)`? | No: it disables NRVO |
| When is `std::move` in return correct? | Members, structured bindings, sub-objects |
| Can I return a `std::mutex`-like type? | Yes as a prvalue (C++17), never by name |
| Is a parameter NRVO'd? | No, moved |
| Does `x = f()` elide? | No: temporary + move assignment |
| Can elision change output? | Yes, explicitly allowed |
| Sink parameter cost? | lvalue: copy+move; rvalue: move(+move); one extra move vs overloads |
| C++23 change? | Returned local names are xvalues (P2266) |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- **RAII** (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): tie a resource to the lifetime of an object.
  - Constructor **acquires** the resource (or throws, so a half-acquired object never exists).
  - Destructor **releases** it.
  - The object's lifetime **is** the ownership: when the object dies, the resource is released, on every exit path.
- "Resource" means anything that must be given back, not only heap memory:

| Resource | Acquire | Release | Standard RAII type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Heap object | `new` | `delete` | `std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr` |
| Heap array / buffer | `new[]` / allocator | `delete[]` / deallocate | `std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr<T[]>` |
| Mutex ownership | `lock()` | `unlock()` | `std::lock_guard`, `std::unique_lock`, `std::scoped_lock` |
| File | `open` / `fopen` | `close` / `fclose` | `std::fstream`, custom wrapper, `unique_ptr<FILE, D>` |
| Thread | start | `join()` | `std::jthread` (C++20) |
| Socket, DB connection, GPU buffer, OS handle | API call | API call | Custom wrapper |

- The RAII object itself is usually an automatic (stack) variable, but it can also be a class member or a container element: then its owner's lifetime decides when it releases.
- RAII does not remove heap allocation; it makes the **release** automatic, deterministic and exception safe.
- Deterministic: release happens at a known point (end of scope), unlike garbage collection or finalizers.

subsections.title: 2. Why manual cleanup fails
subsections.content:
- With `Resource* r = new Resource; ... delete r;` every path that leaves the function must reach `delete`:
  - early `return`, `break`, `continue`, `goto` out of the block
  - any exception thrown by any called function (including `operator new`, `std::string` copies, `vector::push_back`)
  - code added later by someone else
- When the function exits early, the **pointer variable** `r` is destroyed (it is automatic), but the **pointee** is not: nobody owns it any more, so it leaks.
- The manual fix (`try { ... } catch (...) { delete r; throw; }` plus a `delete` before every `return`) does not scale:
  - two resources need nested try blocks
  - a new exit path silently reintroduces the leak
- Leaks are the mild outcome. A forgotten `unlock()` blocks every other thread forever; a forgotten `close()` exhausts descriptors.
- Rule: **no naked `new`/`delete`, no manual `lock()`/`unlock()` in application code**. Every resource is owned by an object from the moment it is acquired.

subsections.title: 3. Stack unwinding: what exactly runs
subsections.content:
- When an exception is thrown and a matching `catch` exists, control transfers to the handler and every **fully constructed automatic object** between the throw point and the handler is destroyed, in reverse order of construction.
- This includes temporaries and partially built arrays/aggregates (elements already constructed are destroyed).
- It does **not** include:
  - heap objects pointed to by raw pointers (the pointer dies, the pointee leaks)
  - objects whose constructor did not complete (their destructor never runs: see section 5)
- When `std::terminate` is called instead, there are **no guarantees**:

| Situation | What happens to automatic objects |
|---|---|
| Exception caught somewhere up the stack | Unwound: destructors run |
| Exception **never caught** | `std::terminate`; implementation-defined whether the stack is unwound. GCC/libstdc++: not unwound, destructors do not run |
| Exception escapes a `noexcept` function | `std::terminate`; stack may be unwound, partially unwound or not at all |
| Destructor throws while another exception is propagating | `std::terminate` |
| `std::exit()` | Automatic objects **not** destroyed; static and `thread_local` objects are |
| `std::abort()`, `std::quick_exit()`, crash, `kill -9` | Nothing destroyed |

- Practical consequence: RAII cleanup is guaranteed only for exceptions that are caught. Long-running programs usually put a top-level `try`/`catch` in `main` and in every thread entry function, so unwinding is guaranteed.
- An exception escaping a `std::thread` entry function calls `std::terminate`; it does not travel to the thread that calls `join()`.

subsections.title: 4. Writing an RAII wrapper
subsections.content:
- Checklist for a wrapper around a raw handle (fd, `FILE*`, socket, C library handle):
  1. Constructor acquires, or **throws** on failure (never leave a "zombie" object that holds an invalid handle and pretends to work), or offer a factory that returns `std::optional`/`expected`.
  2. Destructor releases, is `noexcept` (implicit since C++11), and checks for the "empty" state.
  3. **Decide copy semantics explicitly.** The compiler-generated copy just copies the handle value, so two objects release it twice. Options:
     - Move-only (most handles): delete copy, implement move that leaves the source empty.
     - Deep copy: duplicate the resource (`dup()` for an fd, new allocation for memory).
     - Shared ownership: reference count (`std::shared_ptr` with a custom deleter).
  4. Provide `get()` (observe), `release()` (give up ownership without releasing), `reset()` (release current, adopt new).
  5. Mark the constructor that takes a raw handle `explicit`, so an `int` never silently becomes an owner.
- Rule of 0 first: often the wrapper is just `std::unique_ptr<FILE, Closer>` and needs no hand-written special members. Write the five special members only in the one small class that owns the raw handle (see topic 02 for the Rule of 0/3/5 mechanics and copy-and-swap).
- **Ownership is a contract**, not a property of the handle:
  - `File f(fd);` with `int fd` copies the number 5; the integer has no idea who owns it.
  - The class documentation says "takes ownership": from that line on, the caller must not close `fd`.
  - `std::unique_ptr<int> a(p);` is the same contract for a raw pointer: after it, `delete p` is a double delete.
- Multiple *references* to a resource are fine; multiple *independent owners* are a bug unless ownership is explicitly shared.

subsections.title: 5. Constructors that throw
subsections.content:
- An object's lifetime starts when its constructor **completes**. If the constructor throws:
  - the object never existed, so **its own destructor does not run**
  - every fully constructed **base and member** is destroyed, in reverse order of construction
  - for `new T(...)`, the new-expression calls the matching `operator delete`, so the memory itself does not leak
- Consequence: a class that acquires two raw resources in its constructor leaks the first if acquiring the second throws, because the destructor that would release the first never runs.
- Fix: one resource per RAII member. Then each member that finished construction cleans itself up:

```cpp
// Leaks a_ if the second new throws:
struct Bad  { int* a_; int* b_; Bad() : a_(new int[100]), b_(new int[100]) {} ~Bad(); };
// Correct with zero hand-written cleanup:
struct Good { std::vector<int> a_, b_; Good() : a_(100), b_(100) {} };
```

- Throwing from a constructor is the **correct** way to report failure: there is no return value, and a half-initialized object is worse than no object.
- **Function-try-block** on a constructor catches exceptions from the member initializer list:
  - the handler cannot "rescue" the object: falling off the end of the handler **rethrows** automatically
  - members and bases are already destroyed when the handler runs; touching them is UB
  - legitimate uses: logging, translating the exception type

subsections.title: 6. Destructors must not throw
subsections.content:
- Since C++11 every destructor is implicitly `noexcept(true)` (unless a member or base destructor is `noexcept(false)`).
- So `throw` from a destructor calls `std::terminate` even if the caller has a matching `catch`. GCC warns: "'throw' will always call 'terminate'".
- Even with `noexcept(false)`, a destructor that throws while another exception is propagating calls `std::terminate` (two exceptions in flight).
- Standard containers and algorithms assume non-throwing destructors; a throwing element destructor makes them UB.
- But release operations can fail (`close()` reporting `EIO`, a final flush, a network commit). Pattern:
  - provide an explicit `close()`/`commit()` that **throws or returns an error**, for callers who care
  - the destructor calls the release only if still open, and **swallows or logs** any error
- `std::uncaught_exceptions()` (C++17) lets a destructor know whether it runs because of unwinding (used by scope guards, section 8). The old `std::uncaught_exception()` (singular) was deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20.

subsections.title: 7. Exception safety guarantees
subsections.content:
- Every function should document which guarantee it offers (Abrahams guarantees):

| Guarantee | Promise if an exception escapes | Typical examples |
|---|---|---|
| **No-throw** (`noexcept`) | Never throws | Destructors, `swap`, move ops of most types, `unique_ptr::reset`, `vector::pop_back` |
| **Strong** (commit or rollback) | Program state is exactly as before the call | `vector::push_back` (if move is `noexcept` or copy is used), `map::insert` of one element, copy-and-swap assignment |
| **Basic** | No leaks, invariants hold, objects usable, but the values may have changed | Most functions; `vector::insert` of a range in the middle, `std::sort` on a throwing comparator |
| **None** | Anything: leaks, broken invariants | Bugs; legacy code with raw ownership |

- RAII gives the **basic** guarantee for resources almost for free (no leaks). It does not by itself keep *invariants* between members intact.
- The **strong** guarantee needs a design: do all work that can throw **on the side**, then **commit** with operations that cannot throw:
  - copy-and-swap (topic 02): build a new copy, then `swap` (noexcept)
  - reserve capacity first, then `push_back` with a `noexcept` move
  - write to a temporary file, then `rename` (atomic on POSIX)
- Strong is not always worth its cost: copy-and-swap on a large container copies everything. The standard library itself only gives basic for many range operations. Choose per function.
- The no-throw guarantee is what makes the others possible: you cannot build commit/rollback without at least one operation that cannot fail.
- `vector` growth relies on this: it uses `std::move_if_noexcept`, so an element type with a throwing move constructor gets copied during reallocation (details in topic 02 and topic 03).

subsections.title: 8. Scope guards: RAII for one-off actions
subsections.content:
- Writing a class for every cleanup is heavy. A **scope guard** runs an arbitrary callable when the scope exits:
  - `ScopeGuard g([&] { rollback(); });` and `g.dismiss();` after the commit point.
- Three flavours (names from Library Fundamentals TS v3, `<experimental/scope>`; not in the C++23 standard):

| Guard | Runs callable on |
|---|---|
| `scope_exit` | every exit |
| `scope_fail` | exit by exception only |
| `scope_success` | normal exit only |

- `scope_fail` is implemented by comparing `std::uncaught_exceptions()` at construction and in the destructor. A plain `bool` check (`std::uncaught_exception()`) gave the wrong answer when the guard itself lived inside a destructor that ran during unwinding.
- The callable of a scope guard runs in a destructor: it must not throw.
- Guards are declared **immediately after** the action they undo, so the rollback only exists if the action happened.
- Use a guard for ad hoc rollback in one function; use a named RAII class when the same cleanup appears in several places.

subsections.title: 9. Release order and dependencies
subsections.content:
- Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, locals in reverse definition order (details in topic 01). For RAII this means **declaration order is release order**.
- Declare a resource **after** the resources it depends on:
  - a `std::jthread` member that uses a queue member must be declared after the queue, so it is joined before the queue dies
  - a `lock_guard` must be declared after the mutex it locks (always true for locals, matters for members)
  - a database statement handle after its connection
- `std::unique_ptr` members follow the same rule; `reset()` them explicitly in the destructor body only if you need an order different from declaration order.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "RAII is about heap memory." ✅ It is about any resource with an acquire/release pair: locks, files, sockets, threads.
- ❌ "RAII means we work on the stack instead of the heap." ✅ The *owner* is usually automatic; the resource is often still on the heap.
- ❌ "During unwinding, the `delete` statements of the function run." ✅ Only destructors of automatic objects run; arbitrary statements are skipped.
- ❌ "Destructors are guaranteed to run when an exception is thrown." ✅ Only if it is caught. Uncaught: `std::terminate`, and GCC does not unwind.
- ❌ "If a constructor throws, the destructor cleans up." ✅ The destructor of that object never runs; only its completed members and bases are destroyed.
- ❌ "A destructor may throw if nothing else is in flight." ✅ Destructors are implicitly `noexcept`; a throw calls `std::terminate`.
- ❌ "`File(int fd)` takes ownership because it stores the fd." ✅ Ownership is a documented contract; the compiler-generated copy happily creates a second owner.
- ❌ "Using RAII makes a function strongly exception safe." ✅ RAII prevents leaks (basic guarantee); strong needs do-then-commit design.
- ❌ "`lock_guard` destroys the mutex." ✅ It unlocks the mutex; the mutex lives on.
- ❌ "`std::exit` runs all destructors." ✅ It skips automatic objects; only statics and thread-locals are destroyed.

edge_cases.title: An uncaught exception does not guarantee cleanup
edge_cases.explanation:
- `void work() { Guard g; throw std::runtime_error("boom"); }` called from `main` with no `try`.
- No handler exists, so `std::terminate` is called. Whether the stack is unwound first is **implementation-defined**.
- GCC/libstdc++ does not unwind: `~Guard` never runs; the program prints the terminate message and aborts.
- With a `try`/`catch` around the call, `~Guard` runs before the handler.
- Consequence: cleanup that must happen (flush a log, release an OS-wide lock file) needs a top-level `catch (...)` in `main` and in every thread function.

edge_cases.title: A throwing destructor terminates even inside try/catch
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Bad { ~Bad() { throw std::runtime_error("x"); } };` and `try { Bad b; } catch (...) {}`.
- The destructor is implicitly `noexcept`, so the exception reaches a non-throwing boundary: `std::terminate`.
- The `catch` never runs. GCC warns at compile time: "'throw' will always call 'terminate'".
- Declaring `~Bad() noexcept(false)` makes this one case catchable, but if the destructor runs during unwinding of another exception, it is still `std::terminate`. Do not do it.

edge_cases.title: The constructor throws, the destructor never runs
edge_cases.explanation:
- `Holder() : a_(new int[100]) { init(); }` where `init()` throws.
- `~Holder()` contains `delete[] a_`, but the object never finished construction, so `~Holder` is never called: `a_` leaks.
- Members that are RAII types (already constructed) are destroyed correctly; raw pointers have trivial destructors and release nothing.
- Fix: `std::unique_ptr<int[]> a_` or `std::vector<int> a_`.

edge_cases.title: A copied wrapper closes the handle twice
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct File { int fd; ~File() { close(fd); } };` with no copy control.
- `File b = a;` copies the integer. At scope exit `b` closes fd 3 (succeeds), then `a` closes fd 3 again: `close` returns -1, `EBADF`.
- Worse in a real program: between the two closes another thread may `open` a file and receive the reused number 3, and the second close silently closes **that** unrelated file.
- Fix: delete the copy operations and implement moves that empty the source (or `dup()` for a real copy).

edge_cases.title: Two owners from one raw handle
edge_cases.explanation:
- `int fd = open(...); File a(fd); File b(fd);` compiles even with a move-only `File`: both constructors receive the same integer.
- Same bug as `std::unique_ptr<T> a(p), b(p);`: double release.
- The type system cannot stop it; the contract "constructor takes ownership" must be respected by the caller. Prefer factories that acquire inside the wrapper (`File::open(path)`, `std::make_unique`) so the raw handle is never visible.

edge_cases.title: std::exit skips local destructors
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::exit(0)` from inside a function: static objects and `thread_local`s are destroyed, but locals on the stack (including RAII guards and `unique_ptr`s) are not.
- A `std::lock_guard` held while calling `exit` stays locked; a buffered writer owned by a local is not flushed.
- `return` from `main` runs local destructors of `main`, then calls `exit`. Prefer returning or throwing to `main` over calling `exit` deep in the stack.

edge_cases.title: An exception escaping a noexcept function
edge_cases.explanation:
- `void f() noexcept { throw 1; }` called inside `try { f(); } catch (...) {}`.
- The `catch` is irrelevant: the exception would have to leave a `noexcept` function, so `std::terminate` is called. Unwinding inside `f` may or may not happen.
- Common in practice through **implicitly** noexcept functions: destructors, and move operations or `swap` that were declared `noexcept` but call something that throws.

edge_cases.title: Basic guarantee is not "nothing changed"
edge_cases.explanation:
- `void add(name, weight) { names_.push_back(name); weights_.push_back(check(weight)); }`.
- If `check` throws, nothing leaks (both vectors are RAII), but `names_` has one more element than `weights_`: the class invariant "same size" is broken.
- RAII protected the memory, not the invariant. Reorder (do the throwing work first) or reserve and validate before any visible change.

edge_cases.title: Scope guard dismissed too early
edge_cases.explanation:
- `ScopeGuard undo([&] { book.erase(id); }); undo.dismiss(); notify(id);`
- If `notify` can throw and the order should be rolled back on failure, dismissing before the last throwing step disables the rollback.
- Rule: `dismiss()` is the **last** statement of the transaction, after every operation that can fail.

interview_qa.question: What is RAII, and is it only about heap memory?
interview_qa.answer: RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization) ties a resource to an object's lifetime: the constructor acquires it, the destructor releases it, so release happens automatically on every exit path. It applies to any resource with an acquire/release pair: memory, mutex ownership, files, sockets, threads, OS handles.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Standard examples: `std::unique_ptr`/`std::vector` (memory), `std::lock_guard` (mutex ownership, no heap at all), `std::fstream` (file), `std::jthread` (joins on destruction).
- The owner object is usually automatic (on the stack), but it can be a member or a container element; then its owner decides when it releases.
- RAII does not avoid the heap: `auto p = std::make_unique<R>();` still allocates; RAII makes the **release** automatic.
- Release is **deterministic**: at a known point (end of scope), not "sometime later" like a garbage collector.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "RAII means we work on the stack instead of the heap." The owner is on the stack; the resource is often still on the heap.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "RAII gives deterministic cleanup on normal scope exit, early return and exception-driven unwinding," plus the caveat that unwinding is only guaranteed for caught exceptions.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: RAII = lifetime is ownership, for any resource, not just memory.

interview_qa.question: Why does this function leak, and how does RAII fix it?
interview_qa.answer: On the early `return` or when `doSomething()` throws, `delete[] data` is never reached. interview_qa.question: What is wrong with this locking code, and when exactly is the mutex unlocked in the fixed version?
interview_qa.answer: If `doSomething()` throws, `unlock()` is skipped and `m` stays locked forever; every other thread that needs it blocks indefinitely. interview_qa.question: During stack unwinding, what exactly is destroyed, and what is not?
interview_qa.answer: Every fully constructed automatic object (locals, temporaries, already-built elements and members) between the throw point and the handler is destroyed, in reverse order of construction. Heap objects reached only through raw pointers, and objects whose constructor did not complete, are not destroyed.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Locals of every function being exited, innermost function first.
- Temporaries of the full-expression that threw.
- For an object under construction: its finished bases and members (but not the object's own destructor).
- For an array or aggregate under construction: the elements already constructed.
- Not destroyed: what raw pointers point to, objects with static storage (they die at program exit), objects owned by other threads.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The stack goes out of memory and everything is freed." Unwinding is a precise sequence of destructor calls, not a bulk release.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: unwinding happens only when a handler is found. Without one, `std::terminate` is called and unwinding is implementation-defined.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Unwinding runs destructors of finished automatic objects; anything not owned by such an object is on its own.

interview_qa.question: Is a local object's destructor guaranteed to run if an exception is thrown and never caught?
interview_qa.answer: No. If no matching handler exists, `std::terminate` is called, and whether the stack is unwound before that is implementation-defined. With GCC/libstdc++ the stack is not unwound, so the destructor never runs.

caught boom
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  boom

interview_qa.full_content:

**Explanation:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Guard { ~Guard() { std::cout << "~Guard ran" << std::endl; } };

void work() { Guard g; throw std::runtime_error("boom"); }

int main() {
    try { work(); } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught " << e.what() << std::endl;   // flush: abort won't
    }
    work();   // no handler anywhere
}
```
- Output (GCC 11, Linux):
```
~Guard ran
caught boom
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  boom
```
- The process then aborts (exit status 134, SIGABRT). The second `~Guard ran` never appears.
- `std::endl` matters here: `abort` does not flush `std::cout`, so with output redirected to a file or pipe, unflushed lines are lost too.
- Not unwinding is useful for debugging: the core dump shows the stack at the throw point.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "RAII guarantees cleanup whenever an exception is thrown."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: put `try { ... } catch (...) { log; return 1; }` in `main` and in every thread entry function when cleanup matters (flushing logs, removing lock files, sending a disconnect).

interview_qa.question: Two `File` objects are built from the same file descriptor. What goes wrong?

interview_qa.question: What are the exception safety guarantees, with an example of each?
interview_qa.answer: No-throw: the operation never fails (destructors, `swap`, `unique_ptr::reset`). Strong: if it throws, the state is exactly as before (`vector::push_back`, copy-and-swap assignment). Basic: if it throws, nothing leaks and invariants hold, but values may have changed (most functions, range `vector::insert`). No guarantee: anything can happen (raw owners).
interview_qa.explanation:
- The guarantees form a ladder; each one includes the ones below it.
- RAII alone gives the basic guarantee *for resources*; keeping multi-member invariants needs ordering (see Q12).
- Strong is built **from** no-throw operations: you need at least one step that cannot fail to commit.
- `vector::push_back` gives the strong guarantee only because it copies (rather than moves) elements whose move constructor might throw: `std::move_if_noexcept` (topic 02 and 03).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Exception safe means the function doesn't throw." That is only the strongest level.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: document the guarantee per function; strong is not free (copying), so libraries choose it only where it is cheap or essential.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Each guarantee includes the weaker ones (no-throw includes strong, strong includes basic); RAII gets you basic, design gets you strong.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
No-throw: the operation never fails (destructors, `swap`, `unique_ptr::reset`). Strong: if it throws, the state is exactly as before (`vector::push_back`, copy-and-swap assignment). Basic: if it throws, nothing leaks and invariants hold, but values may have changed (most functions, range `vector::insert`). No guarantee: anything can happen (raw owners).

**Explanation:**
- The guarantees form a ladder; each one includes the ones below it.
- RAII alone gives the basic guarantee *for resources*; keeping multi-member invariants needs ordering (see Q12).
- Strong is built **from** no-throw operations: you need at least one step that cannot fail to commit.
- `vector::push_back` gives the strong guarantee only because it copies (rather than moves) elements whose move constructor might throw: `std::move_if_noexcept` (topic 02 and 03).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Exception safe means the function doesn't throw." That is only the strongest level.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: document the guarantee per function; strong is not free (copying), so libraries choose it only where it is cheap or essential.

**Key takeaway:** Each guarantee includes the weaker ones (no-throw includes strong, strong includes basic); RAII gets you basic, design gets you strong.

interview_qa.question: How do you implement the strong guarantee?
interview_qa.answer: Do all the work that can throw on the side without touching visible state, then commit using only operations that cannot throw. Common forms: copy-and-swap (build a new copy, then `swap`), pre-reserving capacity before `noexcept` moves, writing a temporary file and then `rename`, or a scope guard that rolls back each step.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Copy-and-swap assignment: `T& operator=(T other) noexcept { swap(*this, other); return *this; }`: the copy (which may throw) happens in the parameter, before `*this` changes (topic 02).
- Two containers that must change together: validate, reserve both, then `push_back` with non-throwing moves (theory Example 4).
- Multi-step operations on external systems: scope guards that undo each completed step, dismissed at the commit point (theory Example 5).
- Cost: copy-and-swap on a large object copies all of it even for a small change; sometimes the basic guarantee plus a documented "object is reset on failure" is the better trade.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Wrap the body in try/catch and undo in the catch." Possible, but brittle: the undo code must know exactly how far the body got.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the commit step must be no-throw; if your "commit" can fail, you do not have the strong guarantee.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Strong guarantee = throwing work first, then a no-throw commit.

interview_qa.question: Does using RAII members make a class automatically exception safe?
interview_qa.answer: It guarantees no leaks, but not intact invariants. If a member function changes one member and then throws before changing the related one, every object is still destroyed correctly, yet the class is left in a state that violates its own invariant.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: RAII protects resources; ordering protects invariants.

interview_qa.question: What is a scope guard, and when would you use it instead of a dedicated RAII class?
interview_qa.answer: A scope guard is a small RAII object that runs an arbitrary callable in its destructor, usually with `dismiss()` to cancel it at the commit point. Use it for one-off cleanup or rollback inside a single function; write a named RAII class when the same cleanup is needed in several places.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Typical use: multi-step updates across systems: `step1(); ScopeGuard g1(undo1); step2(); ScopeGuard g2(undo2); step3(); g2.dismiss(); g1.dismiss();`
- Variants (Library Fundamentals TS v3 `<experimental/scope>`): `scope_exit` (always), `scope_fail` (on exception), `scope_success` (on normal exit). Not in C++23; many codebases have their own.
- `scope_fail` compares `std::uncaught_exceptions()` (C++17) at construction and destruction; a plain bool check is wrong when the guard lives inside a destructor running during unwinding.
- The callable runs in a destructor, so it must not throw.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Call `dismiss()` right after the guarded step." Dismiss at the end, after the last operation that can fail.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: declare each guard right after the step it undoes, so rollback runs only for steps that actually happened, in reverse order.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A scope guard is RAII for an action rather than a resource.

interview_qa.question: An exception is thrown inside a `noexcept` function and the caller has a `catch (...)`. What happens?
interview_qa.answer: `std::terminate` is called; the caller's `catch` never runs. When an exception tries to leave a `noexcept` function, the program terminates, and whether the stack inside that function is unwound is implementation-defined.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Throwing out of `noexcept` is not an exception path; it is program termination.

interview_qa.question: Can a constructor's function-try-block catch an exception from a member initializer and keep the object alive?
interview_qa.answer: No. The handler of a constructor's function-try-block runs after all finished members and bases have been destroyed, and when control reaches the end of the handler the exception is automatically rethrown. It can log or translate the exception, nothing more.
code_examples:
handler: member failed
caller: member failed
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A constructor cannot swallow a member's exception; an object whose part failed does not exist.

interview_qa.question: `std::exit(1)` is called deep inside a function holding a `lock_guard` and a `unique_ptr`. Are they cleaned up?
interview_qa.answer: No. `std::exit` does not unwind the stack, so automatic objects (including RAII guards) are not destroyed. It does run `atexit` handlers and destroy objects with static and thread storage duration. `std::abort` and `std::quick_exit` destroy nothing.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `std::exit` skips the stack; only return or a caught exception unwinds it.

interview_qa.question: In what order are an object's resources released, and why does it matter for RAII?
interview_qa.answer: Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order (locals in reverse definition order), so declaration order is release order. A resource that depends on another must be declared after it, so it is released first.
code_examples:
open connection
open statement
close statement
close connection
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Declare dependencies first; RAII releases them last.

interview_qa.question: Your codebase is built with `-fno-exceptions`. How do you keep RAII when a constructor cannot report failure by throwing?
interview_qa.answer: Move the fallible acquisition into a static factory that returns `std::optional<T>` (C++17) or `std::expected<T, E>` (C++23), and make the constructor private and non-failing: it only adopts an already-acquired resource. Every `T` that exists then holds a valid resource, and the destructor still releases it. Avoid the "empty constructor + `bool init()`" pattern, which reintroduces half-built objects.
code_examples:
opened, fd valid: 1
closed
open failed
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Without exceptions, fail in a factory that returns optional/expected; never create a half-initialized object.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
+A +B +C -C -B | +A +B +C -A -C -B
```

**Explanation:**
- Early return: locals are destroyed in reverse order: `c` (prints `-C`), then `b` (its destructor deletes B, prints `-B`). The raw pointer `a` is destroyed too, but destroying a raw pointer does nothing: A leaks.
- Normal path: `delete a` runs as a statement (`-A`), then the locals are destroyed at the closing brace (`-C -B`).
- ASan/LeakSanitizer reports one leaked `Resource` from the first call.
- **Key Concept:** Scope exit destroys owners, not pointees; only objects owned by an RAII object are safe on every path.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
working
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  disk full
(then SIGABRT, exit status 134; ~Guard is NOT printed)
```

**Explanation:**
- No handler exists anywhere, so `std::terminate` is called.
- The standard makes stack unwinding in this case **implementation-defined**. GCC/libstdc++ does not unwind, so `~Guard` never runs.
- Adding `try { work(); } catch (const std::exception&) {}` in `main` changes the output to `working`, `~Guard`, `after work`.
- `std::endl` is used because `abort` does not flush `std::cout`; with `'\n'` and redirected output, even `working` could be lost.
- **Key Concept:** RAII cleanup during exceptions is only guaranteed when the exception is caught; put a top-level handler in `main` and in every thread function.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer:
inspecting fd 3
close(3) -> 0 ok
back in main
close(3) -> -1 Bad file descriptor
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `inspect` takes `File` by value; the implicit copy constructor copies the integer, creating a second owner of fd 3.
- The parameter's destructor closes fd 3 at the end of `inspect`. `log` still holds 3 and closes it again at the end of `main`: `EBADF`.
- In a real program another thread could have opened a file and received number 3 in between: the second close would silently close that file instead.
- fd numbers are typical for a fresh Linux process (0, 1, 2 are taken by stdin, stdout, stderr).
- **Key Concept:** An owning wrapper must define its copy semantics; the default copy of a handle is always a double release.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
+0 +1 -1 -0 | slot 2 failed
```

**Explanation:**
- Array elements are constructed in index order. Elements 0 and 1 complete; element 2 throws before printing.
- The partially constructed array member is unwound: completed elements are destroyed in reverse order (`-1 -0`). Element 3 was never constructed.
- `Pool`'s constructor body never ran and `~Pool` is never called: the `Pool` object never started its lifetime.
- **Key Concept:** Unwinding destroys exactly what finished construction, in reverse order, down to individual array elements.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
~Logger throwing
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  log flush failed
(then SIGABRT)
```

**Explanation:**
- `"order rejected"` starts unwinding; unwinding calls `~Logger`.

- Neither exception is ever caught.
- **Key Concept:** A destructor that can throw turns any exception passing through its scope into program termination; release errors must be swallowed or reported via an explicit call.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
caught: log flush failed
still alive
```

**Explanation:**
- With `noexcept(false)` and no exception in flight, the throw from the destructor propagates normally to the handler.
- Remove `noexcept(false)` and the program terminates instead: destructors are implicitly `noexcept`, and GCC warns "'throw' will always call 'terminate'".
- This "works", but only as long as `Logger` never dies during unwinding (Q5), never lives in a container, and is never a member of something being destroyed by an exception. That is why it is avoided.
- **Key Concept:** `noexcept(false)` destructors are legal and catchable in isolation, and still a design error.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: use after free.
ASan: heap-use-after-free (READ of size 4).
Without sanitizers it printed a garbage number
(glibc reuses the freed block's first bytes for its free list).
```

**Explanation:**
- `load()` returns a temporary `unique_ptr`. It lives until the end of the full expression (the `;` of the declaration), and then its destructor deletes the `Config`.
- `port` refers to a member of the deleted object. Lifetime extension does not apply: the reference binds to a member reached through `operator->`, not to the temporary itself.
- The RAII owner did exactly its job; the bug is a non-owning reference outliving the owner.
- **Key Concept:** RAII releases at the end of the owner's lifetime; a temporary owner's lifetime ends at the semicolon. Keep the owner in a named variable (`auto cfg = load();`), or copy the value (`int port = load()->port;`).

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
allocate 64
deallocate
caught: bad config
```

**Explanation:**
- `new Widget` is two steps: `operator new` (allocate), then the constructor. If the constructor throws, the new-expression itself calls the matching `operator delete` before the exception propagates.
- No leak (ASan clean) and no destructor call: `~Widget` would not run even if it existed.
- The leak risk is different: resources acquired **inside** the constructor before the throw (see theory section 5).
- The class-specific `operator new`/`delete` here are only for tracing; the same happens with the global ones. Overloading allocation functions: topic 10.
- **Key Concept:** A failed constructor in a new-expression frees its storage automatically; what can leak is what the constructor itself acquired.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.answer:
parse error
other thread got the lock: 0
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `doSomething()` throws, `m.unlock()` is skipped, and the exception is caught in `main`. The main thread still owns `m`.
- The other thread's `try_lock` fails. With `lock()` instead it would block forever: the program hangs, with no crash and no error message.
- (`try_lock` can also fail spuriously, but here the mutex really is held.)
- The test uses another thread on purpose: relocking a `std::mutex` from the thread that owns it is UB.
- Fix: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);` in `process()`. During unwinding its destructor unlocks `m`; the other thread prints 1.
- **Key Concept:** Manual `lock()`/`unlock()` around code that can throw is a latent permanent lock; ownership must be an RAII object.

quick_reference.content:
#### RAII wrapper checklist
| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Constructor | Acquire or throw; `explicit` if it adopts a raw handle |
| Destructor | Release if owning; never throws (implicit `noexcept`) |
| Copy | `= delete`, deep copy (`dup`), or shared ownership; never the default for a handle |
| Move | Steal the handle, leave the source empty (`std::exchange(o.h_, invalid)`) |
| Interface | `get()`, `release()`, `reset(new)`, `explicit operator bool` |
| Failing release | Explicit `close()` that reports; destructor logs/swallows |
| Prefer | `unique_ptr<T, Deleter>` when the handle is a pointer (Rule of 0) |

#### What runs on each exit path
| Exit | Automatic objects destroyed? |
|---|---|
| Normal / early `return` / `break` | Yes |
| Exception caught up the stack | Yes (unwinding) |
| Exception never caught | Implementation-defined (GCC: no) |
| Exception escapes `noexcept` | Implementation-defined, then `terminate` |
| Throw from destructor | `terminate` |
| `std::exit` | No (statics yes) |
| `std::abort`, `quick_exit`, crash | No |

#### Exception safety guarantees
| Guarantee | One-line definition | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| No-throw | Cannot fail | `noexcept`, destructors, swap, moves |
| Strong | Success or no change | Do work on the side, commit with no-throw ops; copy-and-swap |
| Basic | No leaks, invariants hold | RAII + ordering |
| None | Anything | Raw owners |

#### Constructor failure
| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Own destructor | Not run |
| Completed members and bases | Destroyed in reverse order |
| Memory from `new T` | Freed by the new-expression |
| Two raw resources in one class | First leaks if second throws: use one RAII member per resource |
| Function-try-block handler | Cannot swallow: rethrows at end; members already gone |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is RAII? | Acquire in constructor, release in destructor; lifetime equals ownership |
| Only memory? | No: locks, files, sockets, threads, any handle |
| Why does raw `new` leak on throw? | The pointer dies during unwinding, the pointee has no owner |
| Destructors guaranteed on throw? | Only if the exception is caught |
| Constructor throws? | Its destructor never runs; finished members are destroyed |
| Can a destructor throw? | Implicitly `noexcept`: `terminate` |
| `close()` can fail? | Explicit `close()` that reports, destructor swallows |
| Basic vs strong? | Basic: valid but maybe changed; strong: unchanged |
| How to get strong? | Throwing work first, commit with no-throw operations |
| Two objects own one fd? | Double close, and the second close can hit a reused fd |
| Scope guard? | RAII for an ad hoc action; dismiss at the commit point |
| `lock_guard` on throw? | Its destructor unlocks the mutex during unwinding |

| `std::exit` | No (statics yes) |
| `std::abort`, `quick_exit`, crash | No |

| Guarantee | One-line definition | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| No-throw | Cannot fail | `noexcept`, destructors, swap, moves |
| Strong | Success or no change | Do work on the side, commit with no-throw ops; copy-and-swap |
| Basic | No leaks, invariants hold | RAII + ordering |
| None | Anything | Raw owners |

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Own destructor | Not run |
| Completed members and bases | Destroyed in reverse order |
| Memory from `new T` | Freed by the new-expression |
| Two raw resources in one class | First leaks if second throws: use one RAII member per resource |
| Function-try-block handler | Cannot swallow: rethrows at end; members already gone |

| Question | Answer |

| What is RAII? | Acquire in constructor, release in destructor; lifetime equals ownership |
| Only memory? | No: locks, files, sockets, threads, any handle |
| Why does raw `new` leak on throw? | The pointer dies during unwinding, the pointee has no owner |
| Destructors guaranteed on throw? | Only if the exception is caught |
| Constructor throws? | Its destructor never runs; finished members are destroyed |
| Can a destructor throw? | Implicitly `noexcept`: `terminate` |
| `close()` can fail? | Explicit `close()` that reports, destructor swallows |
| Basic vs strong? | Basic: valid but maybe changed; strong: unchanged |
| How to get strong? | Throwing work first, commit with no-throw operations |
| Two objects own one fd? | Double close, and the second close can hit a reused fd |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::unique_ptr<T, D = std::default_delete<T>>` (C++11) is **exclusive ownership** of one object (or one array) plus a **cleanup policy**:

```text
unique_ptr<T, D> object (stack, member, container element...)
+---------------------+
| T*  ptr  -----------|------> T object (usually on the heap)
| D   deleter         |        cleanup: deleter(ptr), default: delete ptr
+---------------------+
```

- `p` **is** the `unique_ptr` object; it **contains** a pointer to the managed object. There is no extra pointer to the `unique_ptr`.
- At any moment there is at most one owner. Copy is deleted; ownership can only be **moved**.
- `unique_ptr` does not create the object: `std::make_unique<T>(args...)` (or `new`) creates it, and the `unique_ptr` takes ownership. Its destructor calls the deleter if it owns something.
- Zero overhead in the common case: with the default (stateless) deleter it is exactly one pointer (8 bytes on 64-bit), and `*p`, `p->`, `p.get()` compile to the same code as a raw pointer.
- Use it as the default owning pointer. Reach for `std::shared_ptr` (topic 07) only when ownership is genuinely shared.

subsections.title: 2. Move-only ownership
subsections.content:
- `auto p2 = p1;` does not compile: the copy constructor is deleted ("use of deleted function").
- `auto p2 = std::move(p1);`:
  - `std::move` is only a cast to an rvalue (xvalue); it moves nothing (topic 03)
  - the **move constructor** copies the stored pointer into `p2` and sets `p1`'s pointer to `nullptr`
  - the managed object does not move, is not copied, and no allocation happens
- After the move, `p1` is a valid, **empty** `unique_ptr`. This is **guaranteed** by the standard (unlike most moved-from types, whose state is only "valid but unspecified").
  - `p1 == nullptr`, `!p1`, `p1.get() == nullptr` are all true
  - `p1->f()` or `*p1` is a null dereference: UB
  - `p1` can be reused: `p1 = std::make_unique<T>();`
- Move **assignment** `p1 = std::move(p2);` first takes `p2`'s pointer, then deletes the object `p1` owned before (equivalent to `p1.reset(p2.release())`).
- `sizeof` and type never change with state: a moved-from `unique_ptr<Buffer>` is still a `unique_ptr<Buffer>` of the same size.
- Destruction at scope end: both `p1` and `p2` destructors run, in reverse declaration order (`p2` first). `p2` deletes the object; `p1` holds `nullptr`, so its destructor does nothing. The managed object is destroyed exactly once.

subsections.title: 3. Observers and modifiers
subsections.content:
| Member | Effect | Ownership |
|---|---|---|
| `get()` | Returns the raw pointer | Unchanged (caller only observes) |
| `explicit operator bool` | `get() != nullptr` | Unchanged |
| `*p`, `p->` | Dereference (UB if empty) | Unchanged |
| `release()` | Returns the pointer, sets stored pointer to `nullptr` | **Given up**: caller must free it |
| `reset()` / `reset(nullptr)` | Deletes the owned object, becomes empty | Released |
| `reset(q)` | Stores `q`, then deletes the old object | Takes `q` |
| `swap(other)` | Exchanges pointers and deleters | Swapped |
| `get_deleter()` | Reference to the stored deleter | Unchanged |

- `release()` does **not** delete anything. `p.release();` with the result discarded is a leak (it is not `[[nodiscard]]` in C++20 libstdc++, so the compiler stays silent).
- `reset(q)` order (specified in [unique.ptr.single.modifiers]):
  1. save the old pointer
  2. store `q`
  3. if the old pointer was not null, call the deleter on it
- Why this order: if the old object's destructor reaches back into the owner (`owner.get()`), it sees the new, consistent state instead of a pointer to an object being destroyed. It does not make self-reset safe: `p.reset(p.get())` leaves `p` owning a deleted object (UB).
- `reset()` and the destructor never call the deleter on a null pointer, so a custom deleter is never invoked for an empty `unique_ptr`.
- Comparison with `nullptr` and between `unique_ptr`s compares stored pointers (`operator<=>` since C++20).
- C++23 made `unique_ptr` usable in constant expressions (`constexpr` members).

subsections.title: 4. make_unique and make_unique_for_overwrite
subsections.content:
- `std::make_unique<T>(args...)` (C++14) = `std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...))`.
- Reasons to prefer it:
  - **No naked `new`** in application code: every `new` is immediately owned, and "no `new` outside low-level classes" becomes a reviewable rule.
  - Type is written once: `auto p = std::make_unique<Order>(id, qty);`
  - **Exception safety before C++17**: in `f(std::unique_ptr<A>(new A), g())` a compiler could evaluate `new A`, then `g()`, then construct the `unique_ptr`. If `g()` threw, `A` leaked. `make_unique` performs allocation and ownership in one function call.
- C++17 changed the rules: the initialization of each function parameter is sequenced as a whole (no interleaving), so that specific leak cannot happen any more. The other reasons remain.
- Unlike `make_shared`, `make_unique` gives **no performance benefit**: there is no control block to co-allocate.
- Limitations:
  - no custom deleter: use the constructor `std::unique_ptr<T, D>(ptr, d)`
  - uses parentheses: `make_unique<std::vector<int>>(3, 1)` is `{1, 1, 1}`, not `{3, 1}`
  - aggregates without a constructor work only from C++20 (parenthesized aggregate initialization, P0960)
- Arrays:
  - `make_unique<T[]>(n)`: `new T[n]()`, **value-initialized** (ints zeroed)
  - `make_unique_for_overwrite<T>()` / `<T[]>(n)` (C++20): **default-initialized**, so a large `char` buffer that will be overwritten by `read()` is not zeroed first
  - `make_unique<T[N]>` (known bound) is deleted

subsections.title: 5. Custom deleters
subsections.content:
- The deleter is the cleanup policy: any callable `d(ptr)`. Needed whenever the resource is not released with `delete`:

| Resource | Deleter |
|---|---|
| `FILE*` from `fopen` | `fclose` |
| Memory from `malloc` / C library | `free` |
| C library handle (`sqlite3*`, `SSL*`, `curl*`) | the library's destroy function |
| Object from a pool | return to the pool (stateful deleter) |

- The deleter type is part of the **unique_ptr type**: `unique_ptr<FILE, CloserA>` and `unique_ptr<FILE, CloserB>` are different types, cannot be assigned to each other, and cannot share one `std::vector`. (Contrast: `shared_ptr` type-erases the deleter into the control block, topic 07.)
- `unique_ptr` is therefore **not** type erasure; it is a template that bakes the policy in, which is why it can be zero-overhead.
- Size depends on the deleter (libstdc++ x86-64, verified):

| Deleter | `sizeof(unique_ptr)` | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `default_delete<T>` | 8 | Empty class, stored with empty-base optimization |
| Stateless functor `struct Closer { void operator()(FILE*) const; }` | 8 | Empty |
| Captureless lambda (`decltype(lam)`) | 8 | Empty closure type |
| Function pointer `int(*)(FILE*)` | 16 | Must store the pointer |
| Stateful functor (one `int`) | 16 | Stores its state, padded |
| `std::function<void(T*)>` | 40 | Type-erased callable, heavy |

- Prefer a stateless functor or a lambda type; a function pointer costs 8 bytes and an indirect call per object.
- C++20: a lambda can appear in an unevaluated context, so `std::unique_ptr<FILE, decltype([](FILE* f) { std::fclose(f); })>` works without a named variable.
- `if (f)` inside a `unique_ptr` deleter is harmless but redundant: the deleter is never called with null. (A `shared_ptr` deleter **can** be called with null: `shared_ptr<FILE>(nullptr, d)` calls `d(nullptr)`.)
- Advanced: if the deleter defines `using pointer = X;`, `unique_ptr` stores an `X` instead of `T*` (a "fancy pointer"; it must behave like a nullable pointer).

subsections.title: 6. unique_ptr<T[]>
subsections.content:
- The `T[]` partial specialization uses `default_delete<T[]>`, which calls `delete[]`.
- `std::unique_ptr<int> p(new int[10]);` compiles but pairs `new[]` with scalar `delete`: **UB** (ASan: alloc-dealloc-mismatch). It is not "deletes only the first element"; the language gives no such guarantee.
- `unique_ptr<T[]>` provides `operator[]`, no `operator*`/`operator->`.
- `make_unique<Buffer[]>(5)` constructs 5 `Buffer`s; destruction runs 5 destructors, in reverse index order (4 down to 0).
- No conversion from `unique_ptr<Derived[]>` to `unique_ptr<Base[]>` (pointer arithmetic over a `Base*` into a `Derived` array is wrong). Qualification conversions are allowed (`unique_ptr<int[]>` to `unique_ptr<const int[]>`, C++17).
- It does not know its size. Prefer `std::vector<T>` or `std::array<T, N>`; `unique_ptr<T[]>` fits fixed buffers handed to C APIs or `make_unique_for_overwrite` I/O buffers.

subsections.title: 7. Polymorphism and the virtual destructor
subsections.content:
- Converting move: `std::unique_ptr<Base> b = std::make_unique<Derived>();` compiles because `Derived*` converts to `Base*` and `default_delete<Derived>` converts to `default_delete<Base>`.
- The stored deleter is now `default_delete<Base>`, which calls `delete (Base*)p`.
- If `Base` has **no virtual destructor**, deleting a `Derived` through `Base*` is **UB**: in practice `~Derived` and its members' destructors never run (ASan: new-delete-type-mismatch, e.g. 40 vs 4 bytes).
- Rule: a class meant to be owned polymorphically needs `virtual ~Base() = default;` (or a protected non-virtual destructor to forbid deletion through `Base*`).
- `std::shared_ptr<Base>` created by `make_shared<Derived>()` does call `~Derived` even without a virtual destructor, because its control block captured the right deleter at creation. Do not rely on it; the virtual destructor is still required for every other way of deleting (topic 07).

subsections.title: 8. Passing unique_ptr to and from functions
subsections.content:
- The parameter type documents the ownership intent (Herb Sutter, GotW #91; C++ Core Guidelines R.32 to R.33):

| Signature | Meaning | Caller writes |
|---|---|---|
| `void f(T&)` / `void f(const T&)` | Use the object, no ownership involved | `f(*p)` |
| `void f(T*)` | Use the object, may be null, no ownership | `f(p.get())` |
| `void f(std::unique_ptr<T> p)` | **Sink**: f takes ownership | `f(std::move(p))` |
| `void f(std::unique_ptr<T>& p)` | **Reseat**: f may replace or reset the caller's pointer | `f(p)` |
| `void f(const std::unique_ptr<T>&)` | Almost never useful: use `T&` or `T*` | |
| `std::unique_ptr<T> make()` | **Factory**: caller receives ownership | `auto p = make();` |

- Most functions should not mention `unique_ptr` at all; they operate on `T&`. Ownership appears only where it is transferred.
- Sink by value (not `&&`): the move happens at the call site and is visible; after the call the argument is guaranteed empty.
- Returning a local `unique_ptr` needs no `std::move`: `return p;` uses copy elision or the implicit move on return (topic 04).
- `const std::unique_ptr<T> p` is a non-transferable "scoped pointer": it cannot be moved out or reset; ownership is locked to that scope.

subsections.title: 9. Incomplete types and the pimpl idiom
subsections.content:
- The standard requires `T` to be complete when `default_delete<T>::operator()` is instantiated (libstdc++ enforces it with `static_assert(sizeof(T) > 0)`): `delete` must call the right destructor.
- `unique_ptr<Impl>` itself can be declared with an incomplete `Impl` (that is what makes pimpl work), but every function that may delete must be compiled where `Impl` is complete:
  - the destructor of the owning class
  - its move assignment (deletes the old Impl)
  - its constructors, including the move constructor: a constructor potentially invokes the destructors of already-built members in case a later step throws ([class.base.init]), so an inline `Widget() {}` or `Widget(Widget&&) noexcept = default;` in the header also fails (verified GCC 11, Clang 14)
  - any `reset()` call
- So in pimpl:
  - header: `struct Impl; std::unique_ptr<Impl> impl_;` and **declare** `~Widget();`, `Widget(Widget&&) noexcept;`, `Widget& operator=(Widget&&) noexcept;`
  - .cpp: define `struct Impl { ... };` first, then `Widget::~Widget() = default;` and the moves `= default`
- If the destructor is implicit (inline in the header), it is instantiated in every file that destroys a `Widget`, where `Impl` is incomplete: libstdc++ reports "invalid application of 'sizeof' to incomplete type" from `unique_ptr.h`.
- `shared_ptr<Impl>` does not have this restriction (deleter captured at construction), but costs a control block and atomic counts.

subsections.title: 10. Conversions and ownership hand-off
subsections.content:
- `unique_ptr` to `shared_ptr`: implicit from an rvalue: `std::shared_ptr<T> s = std::move(u);` (or directly from a factory's return value). The custom deleter is moved into the new control block. One extra allocation (the control block), since the object was not created by `make_shared`.
- Therefore factories should return `unique_ptr`: the caller can keep unique ownership, or upgrade to shared for free in terms of API.
- `shared_ptr` to `unique_ptr`: impossible. Other owners may exist; there is no `release()` on `shared_ptr`.
- To a C API that takes ownership: `c_api_adopt(p.release());` (after the call succeeds).
- To a C API that only borrows: `c_api_use(p.get());`.
- Thread safety: same as a raw pointer. Different `unique_ptr` objects can be used from different threads freely; one `unique_ptr` object modified by one thread while another reads it is a data race. The pointee needs its own synchronization.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`std::move(p1)` moves the Resource to `p2`." ✅ Only the stored pointer is transferred; the Resource stays at the same address.
- ❌ "After the move, `p1` is unspecified." ✅ For `unique_ptr` it is guaranteed empty (`nullptr`).
- ❌ "Calling `p1->f()` after the move is safe." ✅ It dereferences null: UB.
- ❌ "`unique_ptr` constructs the object." ✅ `make_unique`/`new` constructs it; `unique_ptr` owns and destroys it.
- ❌ "`unique_ptr<int>(new int[10])` only deletes the first element." ✅ It is UB; use `unique_ptr<int[]>` or `vector`.
- ❌ "`make_unique<Buffer[]>(5)` calls one destructor." ✅ Five, in reverse order.
- ❌ "A custom deleter always increases the size." ✅ Stateless deleters (functor, captureless lambda) add nothing; function pointers and state do.
- ❌ "`unique_ptr` is type-erased like `shared_ptr`." ✅ The deleter is part of the type.
- ❌ "`release()` frees the object." ✅ It gives up ownership and returns the pointer; nothing is freed.
- ❌ "`reset(q)` deletes the old object, then stores `q`." ✅ It stores `q` first, then deletes the old object.
- ❌ "`make_unique` is still needed for exception safety in C++17." ✅ That specific argument-interleaving leak is gone in C++17; `make_unique` is still preferred for no naked `new`.
- ❌ "`unique_ptr<Base>` handles derived destruction automatically." ✅ Only with a virtual destructor in `Base`.
