subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- Every complete object type has two numbers:
  - `sizeof(T)`: bytes the object occupies, including padding. Also the distance between consecutive array elements.
  - `alignof(T)`: the address of every `T` object must be a multiple of this (always a power of two).
- **Alignment is a requirement on addresses; size is a property of the object.** They are related (`sizeof(T)` is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`) but not equal in general: a `struct { char c[7]; }` has size 7 and alignment 1, `long double` on x86-64 has size 16 and alignment 16, `struct { double d; char c; }` has size 16 and alignment 8.
- The compiler inserts **padding** so that every member sits at an offset that is a multiple of its own alignment:
  - **Interior padding**: between members.
  - **Tail padding**: after the last member, so that `sizeof` is a multiple of the struct's alignment and every element of an array stays aligned.
- A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members (and bases), unless raised by `alignas`.
- Layout is **implementation-defined**: the platform ABI (System V x86-64 + Itanium C++ ABI on Linux, the MSVC ABI on Windows) fixes it. Numbers in this topic are for x86-64 Linux with GCC/Clang unless stated.
- Why hardware cares: CPUs load whole aligned words and cache lines. A misaligned value can straddle two words or two cache lines (slower, or a fault on some CPUs), and atomic operations need natural alignment to be atomic at all.

subsections.title: 2. Fundamental types on x86-64
subsections.content:
| Type | sizeof (Linux) | alignof (Linux) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `char`, `bool`, `std::byte` | 1 | 1 | `sizeof(bool)` is implementation-defined, 1 in practice |
| `short` | 2 | 2 | |
| `int`, `float` | 4 | 4 | |
| `long` | 8 | 8 | **4 on Windows (LLP64)** |
| `long long`, `double`, pointers | 8 | 8 | |
| `long double` | 16 | 16 | 8/8 with MSVC |
| `std::max_align_t` | 32 | 16 | Strictest alignment of any scalar type |

- `alignof(std::max_align_t)` (16 here) is the largest "fundamental" alignment. Anything stricter is an **over-aligned** type (e.g. `alignas(64)`).
- `malloc` and plain `operator new` return memory aligned for `max_align_t`; `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__` is 16 on x86-64 Linux.
- Use fixed-width types (`std::uint32_t`, `std::int64_t`) for anything that crosses a process, file or network boundary; `long` changes size between platforms.
- `alignof(T[N]) == alignof(T)`; `sizeof(T[N]) == N * sizeof(T)` (no padding between array elements beyond each element's own tail padding).

subsections.title: 3. Computing a layout by hand
subsections.content:
- Algorithm (what the ABI does):
  1. Start at offset 0.
  2. For each member in declaration order: round the offset up to the member's alignment, place it, advance by its size.
  3. Struct alignment = max member alignment. Round the final offset up to that alignment: that is `sizeof`.
- Worked examples (verified with `offsetof`):

| Struct | Layout | sizeof / alignof |
|---|---|---|
| `struct A { char c; int i; char d; };` | c@0, pad 1-3, i@4, d@8, tail pad 9-11 | 12 / 4 |
| `struct B { int i; char c; char d; };` | i@0, c@4, d@5, tail pad 6-7 | 8 / 4 |
| `struct C1 { char a; double b; char c; int d; };` | a@0, pad, b@8, c@16, pad, d@20 | 24 / 8 |
| `struct C2 { double b; int d; char a; char c; };` | b@0, d@8, a@12, c@13, tail pad | 16 / 8 |
| `struct AM { char c; alignas(16) int x; };` | c@0, pad 1-15, x@16, tail pad 20-31 | 32 / 16 |

- **Why tail padding**: in `A arr[2]`, if `sizeof(A)` were 9, `arr[1].i` would sit at offset 13, not a multiple of 4. Rounding `sizeof` up to 12 keeps every element's members aligned.
- **A struct need not start at a multiple of its size**: `A` (size 12, alignment 4) can live at any address divisible by 4 (100, 104, 108, ...). Its size is a multiple of its alignment, not the other way around.
- A class with virtual functions starts with a vtable pointer (8 bytes, alignment 8): `struct V { virtual ~V(); int x; }` is 16 bytes.
- Bases are laid out like leading members (with the empty-base and tail-padding exceptions in section 8).

subsections.title: 4. Member ordering
subsections.content:
- Compilers **never reorder** non-static data members: addresses increase in declaration order (guaranteed for members with the same access in all standards; for all members since C++23, P1847).
- So padding is in your hands. Rule of thumb: declare members in decreasing order of alignment (8-byte, then 4, 2, 1). `C1` → `C2` saves 8 of 24 bytes (33%).
- Why it matters: 10 million objects at 12 bytes vs 8 bytes is 120 MB vs 80 MB, and more objects per 64-byte cache line means fewer cache misses and less memory bandwidth in scans.
- It is a heuristic, not a law. Other forces:
  - **Hot/cold grouping**: put fields the hot path touches together (ideally in the first cache line), even at the cost of a few padding bytes.
  - **ABI stability**: reordering members of a public or wire/shared-memory struct breaks binary compatibility.
  - Readability and logical grouping.
- Tools: `-Wpadded` (GCC/Clang warn on every padding insertion), `pahole` (shows holes in a compiled binary), `static_assert(sizeof(T) == N)` to lock the result.

subsections.title: 5. alignas and over-aligned types
subsections.content:
- `alignas(N)` (C++11) can be applied to a variable, a non-static data member, or a class:
  - `alignas(64) std::atomic<long> counter;`: this variable is 64-aligned.
  - `struct S { char c; alignas(16) int x; };`: member at offset 16, struct alignment 16.
  - `struct alignas(64) Line { int x; };`: `alignof` 64 and `sizeof` rounded up to 64.
  - `alignas(T)` (a type) means `alignas(alignof(T))`.
- Rules:
  - `N` must be a power of two (GCC: "requested alignment '3' is not a positive power of 2").
  - It can only **strengthen** alignment. Requesting less than the natural alignment is ill-formed: Clang errors ("requested alignment is less than minimum alignment of 4 for type 'int'"), GCC silently ignores it (`alignof` stays 4). Use packing to weaken alignment, not `alignas`.
  - With several `alignas` on one entity the strictest wins; `alignas(0)` is ignored.
- Where over-aligned objects come from:
  - Static and automatic storage: the compiler aligns them (it realigns the stack if needed).
  - Dynamic storage: since C++17 `new T` for an over-aligned `T` calls `operator new(size_t, std::align_val_t)`, so `new`, `std::make_unique`, `std::vector<T>` all return properly aligned memory. Before C++17 over-alignment on the heap was not guaranteed (a classic bug with SIMD types in containers). Details: topic 10.
  - `std::aligned_alloc` (C++17, from C11) for raw memory.
- Helpers:
  - `std::align(alignment, size, ptr, space)`: bumps `ptr` forward to the next aligned address inside a buffer and shrinks `space`; returns `nullptr` if it does not fit. Used by arenas.
  - `std::assume_aligned<N>(p)` (C++20): promises the optimizer that `p` is N-aligned (wrong promise = UB).
  - `std::aligned_storage` / `aligned_union`: deprecated in C++23; write `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)];` instead.

subsections.title: 6. Packed structs and misaligned access
subsections.content:
- Packing removes padding by lowering member alignment:
  - `#pragma pack(push, 1)` ... `#pragma pack(pop)` (MSVC, GCC, Clang).
  - `struct __attribute__((packed)) P { ... };` (GCC/Clang).
  - `struct { char c; int i; }` packed: size 5, alignment 1, `i` at offset 1.
- Consequences:
  - Members are misaligned. The compiler knows this when you access `p.i` directly, so it emits safe (possibly slower) code.
  - A pointer or reference to a packed member loses that knowledge: `int& r = p.i;` claims an aligned `int`. GCC rejects it for `__attribute__((packed))` ("cannot bind packed field 'p.P::i' to 'int&'") and warns for pointers (`-Waddress-of-packed-member`); Clang 14 also warns for the pointer but accepts the reference silently; with `#pragma pack` GCC 11 and Clang 14 accepted both silently.
  - Atomics, SIMD loads and some CPUs (older ARM, SPARC) require alignment: misaligned access may be non-atomic or fault. On x86 a misaligned locked instruction that crosses a cache line is a "split lock" (very slow, can be trapped by the OS).
  - Arrays of packed structs put most elements at odd addresses.
- Misaligned access through a normal pointer (`*reinterpret_cast<int*>(buf + 1)`) is **undefined behaviour**, even on x86 where it usually "works". UBSan: "store to misaligned address ... for type 'int', which requires 4 byte alignment".
- Portable way to read a field from a byte buffer: `std::memcpy(&value, buf + offset, sizeof value);` (compilers turn it into a single load) or `std::bit_cast` for a whole object. Reinterpreting bytes as objects is topic 10 (`start_lifetime_as`, strict aliasing).
- Wire formats: prefer explicit (de)serialization with fixed-width types and explicit byte order (`std::endian` C++20, `std::byteswap` C++23) over overlaying a packed struct onto the buffer.

subsections.title: 7. Locking a layout and padding bytes
subsections.content:
- Lock assumptions at compile time so a later edit cannot silently change a binary layout:
  - `static_assert(sizeof(Header) == 16);`
  - `static_assert(alignof(Header) == 8);`
  - `static_assert(offsetof(Header, seq) == 8);`
  - `static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Header>);` (safe to `memcpy`)
  - `static_assert(std::is_standard_layout_v<Header>);` (C-compatible layout, first member at offset 0, `offsetof` well-defined)
- `offsetof` on a non-standard-layout type (virtual functions, mixed access with members, etc.) is conditionally-supported: GCC warns `-Winvalid-offsetof`.
- **Padding bytes have unspecified values.** Consequences:
  - `memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a)` can report "different" for objects with equal members.
  - Hashing raw bytes of a padded struct hashes garbage.
  - Writing a padded struct to a file or socket leaks whatever was in the padding (an information-leak bug class in kernels).
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` (C++17) is true only if equal values imply equal bytes: no padding, no floats (two zeros, NaNs). Verified: `A` and `B` above are false, `struct { int a; int b; }` is true, `float` is false.
- Compare members, not bytes: C++20 `bool operator==(const T&) const = default;`.

subsections.title: 8. Empty classes, EBO, [[no_unique_address]] and tail-padding reuse
subsections.content:
- An empty class (`struct E {};`) has `sizeof(E) == 1`: two distinct objects must have distinct addresses.
- As a **member**, an empty class costs its byte plus padding: `struct M { E e; int x; }` is 8.
- As a **base**, it can take zero bytes: **empty base optimization** (EBO). `struct D : E { int x; }` is 4. Mandatory for standard-layout classes, universal in practice.
- EBO is blocked when two subobjects of the same empty type would share an address: `struct D2 : E { E e; int x; }` is 8.
- `[[no_unique_address]]` (C++20) gives members the same treatment: `struct N { [[no_unique_address]] E e; int x; }` is 4.
  - Two `[[no_unique_address]]` members of the same empty type still need distinct addresses (GCC placed them at offsets 0 and 1, overlapping `x`; size stayed 4).
  - MSVC ignores the standard attribute for ABI reasons; it needs `[[msvc::no_unique_address]]`.
- Where it matters: stateless allocators, deleters, comparators and policies stored inside containers and smart pointers. This is why `std::unique_ptr<T>` with a stateless deleter is 8 bytes (topic 06).
- **Tail-padding reuse** (Itanium ABI): a derived class may place its members inside the tail padding of a base that is not "POD for layout" (e.g. has a user-provided constructor):
  - `struct Base { int x; char c; Base() {} }; struct Der : Base { char d; };` → `sizeof(Der) == 8` (`d` at offset 5).
  - Same members but `Base` is an aggregate → `sizeof(Der) == 12`.
  - Consequence: `memcpy(base_ptr, src, sizeof(Base))` into a base subobject can overwrite the derived class's members. Copying a base subobject with `memcpy` is not allowed even for trivially copyable types (it is a potentially-overlapping subobject).

subsections.title: 9. Bit-fields
subsections.content:
- `unsigned flags : 3;` declares a member occupying 3 bits of an "allocation unit" of the declared type.
- What is implementation-defined: allocation order within the unit (low-to-high on x86-64 Linux, may differ elsewhere), whether a field can straddle units, signedness of plain `int` bit-fields (only before C++14; CWG 739 made them signed), padding between units. Never use bit-fields to describe a wire or hardware register format portably.
- Properties:
  - Cannot take the address (`&s.flags`: "attempt to take address of bit-field") or bind a non-const reference.
  - Assigning an out-of-range value to an unsigned bit-field keeps the low bits (GCC: `-Woverflow` "changes value from '9' to '1'").
  - A signed 1-bit field holds 0 and -1, not 0 and 1.
  - `unsigned : 0;` (unnamed, width 0) forces the next bit-field into a new allocation unit.
  - `struct { unsigned a:3; unsigned b:5; unsigned c:24; }` is 4 bytes; `struct { bool f1:1; bool f2:1; }` is 1 byte.
- **Concurrency**: a sequence of adjacent non-zero-width bit-fields is a single **memory location**. Two threads writing *different* bit-fields of the same struct without synchronization is a **data race** (verified: TSan reports it). Separate them with a non-bit-field member or a `:0` field, or protect them together.
- Reads and writes compile to load/mask/shift/store sequences: compact but not free.

subsections.title: 10. Layout and performance (short; depth in the Systems chapter)
subsections.content:
- Cache line: 64 bytes on mainstream x86-64 and most ARM. Smaller structs = more objects per line = fewer misses in scans.
- **Hot/cold splitting**: keep fields used on every message in one line; move rarely used fields to a separate struct or behind a pointer.
- **AoS vs SoA**:
  - Array of Structures (`std::vector<Quote>`): good when the hot loop uses most fields of each object.
  - Structure of Arrays (`std::vector<double> bid, ask, ...`): good when the loop uses one or two fields across many objects (every byte loaded is useful, SIMD-friendly contiguous data).
  - Choose by access pattern; the Systems chapter covers measurements.
- **False sharing**: two threads writing different variables that share one cache line make the line bounce between cores. Fix: give each hot variable its own line with `alignas(64)` (struct with two such counters: 128 bytes).
- `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` / `hardware_constructive_interference_size` (C++17, `<new>`): portable constants for this. Library support arrived late (libstdc++ in GCC 12, which warns `-Winterference-size` because the value may differ between `-mtune` targets); GCC 11 does not define them, so code often falls back to 64.
- Padding to a cache line wastes memory; use it for a few hot, contended objects (queue indices, per-thread counters, shard locks), not for millions of small objects.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "An address must be divisible by `sizeof(T)`." ✅ By `alignof(T)`; they coincide only for some scalars.
- ❌ "`sizeof(struct)` is a multiple of its largest member's size." ✅ A multiple of the struct's alignment.
- ❌ "A 12-byte struct must start at a multiple of 12." ✅ At a multiple of its alignment (4).
- ❌ "Padding exists to keep the struct in one cache line." ✅ Padding satisfies alignment; cache-line placement is a separate, explicit choice (`alignas(64)`).
- ❌ "The compiler reorders members to minimise padding." ✅ C++ compilers never reorder data members; you must order them.
- ❌ "`alignas(1)` packs a struct." ✅ `alignas` can only increase alignment; packing needs `#pragma pack` or `__attribute__((packed))`.
- ❌ "Misaligned access is fine on x86." ✅ It is UB in C++, slower across cache lines, non-atomic for atomics, and faults on other CPUs.
- ❌ "`memcmp` is a fast, correct equality for structs." ✅ Padding bytes are unspecified; compare members or use `= default` `operator==`.
- ❌ "An empty member costs nothing." ✅ It costs at least one byte plus padding unless it is a base or `[[no_unique_address]]`.
- ❌ "Different bit-fields can be written by different threads." ✅ Adjacent bit-fields form one memory location: that is a data race.
- ❌ "SoA is always faster than AoS." ✅ It depends on which fields the hot loop touches.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- Every complete object type has two numbers:
  - `sizeof(T)`: bytes the object occupies, including padding. Also the distance between consecutive array elements.
  - `alignof(T)`: the address of every `T` object must be a multiple of this (always a power of two).
- **Alignment is a requirement on addresses; size is a property of the object.** They are related (`sizeof(T)` is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`) but not equal in general: a `struct { char c[7]; }` has size 7 and alignment 1, `long double` on x86-64 has size 16 and alignment 16, `struct { double d; char c; }` has size 16 and alignment 8.
- The compiler inserts **padding** so that every member sits at an offset that is a multiple of its own alignment:
  - **Interior padding**: between members.
  - **Tail padding**: after the last member, so that `sizeof` is a multiple of the struct's alignment and every element of an array stays aligned.
- A struct's alignment is the largest alignment of its members (and bases), unless raised by `alignas`.
- Layout is **implementation-defined**: the platform ABI (System V x86-64 + Itanium C++ ABI on Linux, the MSVC ABI on Windows) fixes it. Numbers in this topic are for x86-64 Linux with GCC/Clang unless stated.
- Why hardware cares: CPUs load whole aligned words and cache lines. A misaligned value can straddle two words or two cache lines (slower, or a fault on some CPUs), and atomic operations need natural alignment to be atomic at all.

#### 2. Fundamental types on x86-64
| Type | sizeof (Linux) | alignof (Linux) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| `char`, `bool`, `std::byte` | 1 | 1 | `sizeof(bool)` is implementation-defined, 1 in practice |
| `short` | 2 | 2 | |
| `int`, `float` | 4 | 4 | |
| `long` | 8 | 8 | **4 on Windows (LLP64)** |
| `long long`, `double`, pointers | 8 | 8 | |
| `long double` | 16 | 16 | 8/8 with MSVC |
| `std::max_align_t` | 32 | 16 | Strictest alignment of any scalar type |

- `alignof(std::max_align_t)` (16 here) is the largest "fundamental" alignment. Anything stricter is an **over-aligned** type (e.g. `alignas(64)`).
- `malloc` and plain `operator new` return memory aligned for `max_align_t`; `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__` is 16 on x86-64 Linux.
- Use fixed-width types (`std::uint32_t`, `std::int64_t`) for anything that crosses a process, file or network boundary; `long` changes size between platforms.
- `alignof(T[N]) == alignof(T)`; `sizeof(T[N]) == N * sizeof(T)` (no padding between array elements beyond each element's own tail padding).

#### 3. Computing a layout by hand
- Algorithm (what the ABI does):
  1. Start at offset 0.
  2. For each member in declaration order: round the offset up to the member's alignment, place it, advance by its size.
  3. Struct alignment = max member alignment. Round the final offset up to that alignment: that is `sizeof`.
- Worked examples (verified with `offsetof`):

| Struct | Layout | sizeof / alignof |
|---|---|---|
| `struct A { char c; int i; char d; };` | c@0, pad 1-3, i@4, d@8, tail pad 9-11 | 12 / 4 |
| `struct B { int i; char c; char d; };` | i@0, c@4, d@5, tail pad 6-7 | 8 / 4 |
| `struct C1 { char a; double b; char c; int d; };` | a@0, pad, b@8, c@16, pad, d@20 | 24 / 8 |
| `struct C2 { double b; int d; char a; char c; };` | b@0, d@8, a@12, c@13, tail pad | 16 / 8 |
| `struct AM { char c; alignas(16) int x; };` | c@0, pad 1-15, x@16, tail pad 20-31 | 32 / 16 |

- **Why tail padding**: in `A arr[2]`, if `sizeof(A)` were 9, `arr[1].i` would sit at offset 13, not a multiple of 4. Rounding `sizeof` up to 12 keeps every element's members aligned.
- **A struct need not start at a multiple of its size**: `A` (size 12, alignment 4) can live at any address divisible by 4 (100, 104, 108, ...). Its size is a multiple of its alignment, not the other way around.
- A class with virtual functions starts with a vtable pointer (8 bytes, alignment 8): `struct V { virtual ~V(); int x; }` is 16 bytes.
- Bases are laid out like leading members (with the empty-base and tail-padding exceptions in section 8).

#### 4. Member ordering
- Compilers **never reorder** non-static data members: addresses increase in declaration order (guaranteed for members with the same access in all standards; for all members since C++23, P1847).
- So padding is in your hands. Rule of thumb: declare members in decreasing order of alignment (8-byte, then 4, 2, 1). `C1` → `C2` saves 8 of 24 bytes (33%).
- Why it matters: 10 million objects at 12 bytes vs 8 bytes is 120 MB vs 80 MB, and more objects per 64-byte cache line means fewer cache misses and less memory bandwidth in scans.
- It is a heuristic, not a law. Other forces:
  - **Hot/cold grouping**: put fields the hot path touches together (ideally in the first cache line), even at the cost of a few padding bytes.
  - **ABI stability**: reordering members of a public or wire/shared-memory struct breaks binary compatibility.
  - Readability and logical grouping.
- Tools: `-Wpadded` (GCC/Clang warn on every padding insertion), `pahole` (shows holes in a compiled binary), `static_assert(sizeof(T) == N)` to lock the result.

#### 5. alignas and over-aligned types
- `alignas(N)` (C++11) can be applied to a variable, a non-static data member, or a class:
  - `alignas(64) std::atomic<long> counter;`: this variable is 64-aligned.
  - `struct S { char c; alignas(16) int x; };`: member at offset 16, struct alignment 16.
  - `struct alignas(64) Line { int x; };`: `alignof` 64 and `sizeof` rounded up to 64.
  - `alignas(T)` (a type) means `alignas(alignof(T))`.
- Rules:
  - `N` must be a power of two (GCC: "requested alignment '3' is not a positive power of 2").
  - It can only **strengthen** alignment. Requesting less than the natural alignment is ill-formed: Clang errors ("requested alignment is less than minimum alignment of 4 for type 'int'"), GCC silently ignores it (`alignof` stays 4). Use packing to weaken alignment, not `alignas`.
  - With several `alignas` on one entity the strictest wins; `alignas(0)` is ignored.
- Where over-aligned objects come from:
  - Static and automatic storage: the compiler aligns them (it realigns the stack if needed).
  - Dynamic storage: since C++17 `new T` for an over-aligned `T` calls `operator new(size_t, std::align_val_t)`, so `new`, `std::make_unique`, `std::vector<T>` all return properly aligned memory. Before C++17 over-alignment on the heap was not guaranteed (a classic bug with SIMD types in containers). Details: topic 10.
  - `std::aligned_alloc` (C++17, from C11) for raw memory.
- Helpers:
  - `std::align(alignment, size, ptr, space)`: bumps `ptr` forward to the next aligned address inside a buffer and shrinks `space`; returns `nullptr` if it does not fit. Used by arenas.
  - `std::assume_aligned<N>(p)` (C++20): promises the optimizer that `p` is N-aligned (wrong promise = UB).
  - `std::aligned_storage` / `aligned_union`: deprecated in C++23; write `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)];` instead.

#### 6. Packed structs and misaligned access
- Packing removes padding by lowering member alignment:
  - `#pragma pack(push, 1)` ... `#pragma pack(pop)` (MSVC, GCC, Clang).
  - `struct __attribute__((packed)) P { ... };` (GCC/Clang).
  - `struct { char c; int i; }` packed: size 5, alignment 1, `i` at offset 1.
- Consequences:
  - Members are misaligned. The compiler knows this when you access `p.i` directly, so it emits safe (possibly slower) code.
  - A pointer or reference to a packed member loses that knowledge: `int& r = p.i;` claims an aligned `int`. GCC rejects it for `__attribute__((packed))` ("cannot bind packed field 'p.P::i' to 'int&'") and warns for pointers (`-Waddress-of-packed-member`); Clang 14 also warns for the pointer but accepts the reference silently; with `#pragma pack` GCC 11 and Clang 14 accepted both silently.
  - Atomics, SIMD loads and some CPUs (older ARM, SPARC) require alignment: misaligned access may be non-atomic or fault. On x86 a misaligned locked instruction that crosses a cache line is a "split lock" (very slow, can be trapped by the OS).
  - Arrays of packed structs put most elements at odd addresses.
- Misaligned access through a normal pointer (`*reinterpret_cast<int*>(buf + 1)`) is **undefined behaviour**, even on x86 where it usually "works". UBSan: "store to misaligned address ... for type 'int', which requires 4 byte alignment".
- Portable way to read a field from a byte buffer: `std::memcpy(&value, buf + offset, sizeof value);` (compilers turn it into a single load) or `std::bit_cast` for a whole object. Reinterpreting bytes as objects is topic 10 (`start_lifetime_as`, strict aliasing).
- Wire formats: prefer explicit (de)serialization with fixed-width types and explicit byte order (`std::endian` C++20, `std::byteswap` C++23) over overlaying a packed struct onto the buffer.

#### 7. Locking a layout and padding bytes
- Lock assumptions at compile time so a later edit cannot silently change a binary layout:
  - `static_assert(sizeof(Header) == 16);`
  - `static_assert(alignof(Header) == 8);`
  - `static_assert(offsetof(Header, seq) == 8);`
  - `static_assert(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Header>);` (safe to `memcpy`)
  - `static_assert(std::is_standard_layout_v<Header>);` (C-compatible layout, first member at offset 0, `offsetof` well-defined)
- `offsetof` on a non-standard-layout type (virtual functions, mixed access with members, etc.) is conditionally-supported: GCC warns `-Winvalid-offsetof`.
- **Padding bytes have unspecified values.** Consequences:
  - `memcmp(&a, &b, sizeof a)` can report "different" for objects with equal members.
  - Hashing raw bytes of a padded struct hashes garbage.
  - Writing a padded struct to a file or socket leaks whatever was in the padding (an information-leak bug class in kernels).
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` (C++17) is true only if equal values imply equal bytes: no padding, no floats (two zeros, NaNs). Verified: `A` and `B` above are false, `struct { int a; int b; }` is true, `float` is false.
- Compare members, not bytes: C++20 `bool operator==(const T&) const = default;`.

#### 8. Empty classes, EBO, [[no_unique_address]] and tail-padding reuse
- An empty class (`struct E {};`) has `sizeof(E) == 1`: two distinct objects must have distinct addresses.
- As a **member**, an empty class costs its byte plus padding: `struct M { E e; int x; }` is 8.
- As a **base**, it can take zero bytes: **empty base optimization** (EBO). `struct D : E { int x; }` is 4. Mandatory for standard-layout classes, universal in practice.
- EBO is blocked when two subobjects of the same empty type would share an address: `struct D2 : E { E e; int x; }` is 8.
- `[[no_unique_address]]` (C++20) gives members the same treatment: `struct N { [[no_unique_address]] E e; int x; }` is 4.
  - Two `[[no_unique_address]]` members of the same empty type still need distinct addresses (GCC placed them at offsets 0 and 1, overlapping `x`; size stayed 4).
  - MSVC ignores the standard attribute for ABI reasons; it needs `[[msvc::no_unique_address]]`.
- Where it matters: stateless allocators, deleters, comparators and policies stored inside containers and smart pointers. This is why `std::unique_ptr<T>` with a stateless deleter is 8 bytes (topic 06).
- **Tail-padding reuse** (Itanium ABI): a derived class may place its members inside the tail padding of a base that is not "POD for layout" (e.g. has a user-provided constructor):
  - `struct Base { int x; char c; Base() {} }; struct Der : Base { char d; };` → `sizeof(Der) == 8` (`d` at offset 5).
  - Same members but `Base` is an aggregate → `sizeof(Der) == 12`.
  - Consequence: `memcpy(base_ptr, src, sizeof(Base))` into a base subobject can overwrite the derived class's members. Copying a base subobject with `memcpy` is not allowed even for trivially copyable types (it is a potentially-overlapping subobject).

#### 9. Bit-fields
- `unsigned flags : 3;` declares a member occupying 3 bits of an "allocation unit" of the declared type.
- What is implementation-defined: allocation order within the unit (low-to-high on x86-64 Linux, may differ elsewhere), whether a field can straddle units, signedness of plain `int` bit-fields (only before C++14; CWG 739 made them signed), padding between units. Never use bit-fields to describe a wire or hardware register format portably.
- Properties:
  - Cannot take the address (`&s.flags`: "attempt to take address of bit-field") or bind a non-const reference.
  - Assigning an out-of-range value to an unsigned bit-field keeps the low bits (GCC: `-Woverflow` "changes value from '9' to '1'").
  - A signed 1-bit field holds 0 and -1, not 0 and 1.
  - `unsigned : 0;` (unnamed, width 0) forces the next bit-field into a new allocation unit.
  - `struct { unsigned a:3; unsigned b:5; unsigned c:24; }` is 4 bytes; `struct { bool f1:1; bool f2:1; }` is 1 byte.
- **Concurrency**: a sequence of adjacent non-zero-width bit-fields is a single **memory location**. Two threads writing *different* bit-fields of the same struct without synchronization is a **data race** (verified: TSan reports it). Separate them with a non-bit-field member or a `:0` field, or protect them together.
- Reads and writes compile to load/mask/shift/store sequences: compact but not free.

#### 10. Layout and performance (short; depth in the Systems chapter)
- Cache line: 64 bytes on mainstream x86-64 and most ARM. Smaller structs = more objects per line = fewer misses in scans.
- **Hot/cold splitting**: keep fields used on every message in one line; move rarely used fields to a separate struct or behind a pointer.
- **AoS vs SoA**:
  - Array of Structures (`std::vector<Quote>`): good when the hot loop uses most fields of each object.
  - Structure of Arrays (`std::vector<double> bid, ask, ...`): good when the loop uses one or two fields across many objects (every byte loaded is useful, SIMD-friendly contiguous data).
  - Choose by access pattern; the Systems chapter covers measurements.
- **False sharing**: two threads writing different variables that share one cache line make the line bounce between cores. Fix: give each hot variable its own line with `alignas(64)` (struct with two such counters: 128 bytes).
- `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` / `hardware_constructive_interference_size` (C++17, `<new>`): portable constants for this. Library support arrived late (libstdc++ in GCC 12, which warns `-Winterference-size` because the value may differ between `-mtune` targets); GCC 11 does not define them, so code often falls back to 64.
- Padding to a cache line wastes memory; use it for a few hot, contended objects (queue indices, per-thread counters, shard locks), not for millions of small objects.

#### 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "An address must be divisible by `sizeof(T)`." ✅ By `alignof(T)`; they coincide only for some scalars.
- ❌ "`sizeof(struct)` is a multiple of its largest member's size." ✅ A multiple of the struct's alignment.
- ❌ "A 12-byte struct must start at a multiple of 12." ✅ At a multiple of its alignment (4).
- ❌ "Padding exists to keep the struct in one cache line." ✅ Padding satisfies alignment; cache-line placement is a separate, explicit choice (`alignas(64)`).
- ❌ "The compiler reorders members to minimise padding." ✅ C++ compilers never reorder data members; you must order them.
- ❌ "`alignas(1)` packs a struct." ✅ `alignas` can only increase alignment; packing needs `#pragma pack` or `__attribute__((packed))`.
- ❌ "Misaligned access is fine on x86." ✅ It is UB in C++, slower across cache lines, non-atomic for atomics, and faults on other CPUs.
- ❌ "`memcmp` is a fast, correct equality for structs." ✅ Padding bytes are unspecified; compare members or use `= default` `operator==`.
- ❌ "An empty member costs nothing." ✅ It costs at least one byte plus padding unless it is a base or `[[no_unique_address]]`.
- ❌ "Different bit-fields can be written by different threads." ✅ Adjacent bit-fields form one memory location: that is a data race.
- ❌ "SoA is always faster than AoS." ✅ It depends on which fields the hot loop touches.

edge_cases.title: Alignment is not size
edge_cases.explanation:
- `sizeof(int) == alignof(int) == 4` on x86-64, which makes "divisible by size" look correct. It breaks for aggregates and some scalars:
  - `struct { char c[7]; }`: size 7, alignment 1.
  - `struct { double d; char c; }`: size 16, alignment 8.
  - `long double`: 16/16 on x86-64 Linux, but 8/8 with MSVC; and 12/4 on 32-bit x86 Linux.
- The correct rules are always stated with `alignof`: member offsets are multiples of the member's alignment, and `sizeof` is a multiple of the struct's alignment.

edge_cases.title: Tail padding counts, even with no member after it
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct B { int i; char c; char d; };` uses 6 bytes of data but `sizeof(B) == 8`.
- `sizeof` must be the array stride, and the stride must keep `arr[1].i` aligned.
- Consequence: `malloc(6)` for a `B`, or writing `B` to a socket with a hand-computed length of 6, is wrong; always use `sizeof`.

edge_cases.title: memcmp and hashing over padding
edge_cases.explanation:
- Two objects with equal members can differ in their padding bytes, so `memcmp` says "not equal" and a byte-wise hash puts them in different buckets.
- Zeroed padding is only promised by zero-initialization (statics; value-initialization of a non-aggregate without a user-provided constructor). `T x{}` on a plain aggregate usually zeroes it in practice but does not promise it, and later member assignments and copies do not have to preserve padding values.
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` tells you whether byte-wise comparison/hashing is valid for `T`.
- Sending a padded struct over the network or into a file also leaks stale stack or heap bytes.

edge_cases.title: References and pointers into packed structs
edge_cases.explanation:
- `#pragma pack(1) struct P { char c; int i; };` places `i` at offset 1.
- `int& r = p.i;` or `int* q = &p.i;` produce a "normal" `int` reference/pointer to a misaligned address; any later use is UB and can fault on strict-alignment CPUs or with SIMD/atomics.
- Diagnostics are inconsistent: with `__attribute__((packed))` GCC refuses the reference and warns for the pointer (Clang 14 warns for the pointer only); with `#pragma pack` GCC 11 and Clang 14 said nothing.
- Copy the value out (`int v = p.i;`) instead of taking its address.

edge_cases.title: Casting a byte buffer to a struct pointer
edge_cases.explanation:
- `auto* h = reinterpret_cast<const Header*>(buf + 3);` is wrong twice:
  - Misalignment: `buf + 3` is not aligned for `Header` (UB; UBSan reports "misaligned address").
  - Lifetime/aliasing: no `Header` object exists there (topic 10: `std::start_lifetime_as`, strict aliasing).
- It "works" on x86 in tests and breaks on ARM, under optimisation, or under sanitizers.
- Fix: `Header h; std::memcpy(&h, buf + 3, sizeof h);` (one or two loads after optimisation).

edge_cases.title: alignas that is silently ignored, or rejected
edge_cases.explanation:
- `alignas(1) int x;` asks for less than the natural alignment: ill-formed. Clang: error; GCC 11: accepted and ignored (`alignof` remains 4).
- `alignas(3)`: error on all compilers (not a power of two).
- `alignas(64)` on a struct makes `sizeof` at least 64: an array of 1000 such structs uses 64 KB even if each holds one `int`.
- `alignas` on a typedef or a function parameter is not allowed; put it on the variable, member or class.

edge_cases.title: EBO fails, or does not exist on one compiler
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct D2 : E { E e; int x; };` is 8 bytes on GCC: the base `E` and member `e` are distinct objects of the same type and must have distinct addresses.
- Two `[[no_unique_address]]` members of the same empty type also need distinct addresses.
- MSVC ignores `[[no_unique_address]]` (needs `[[msvc::no_unique_address]]`) and applies EBO only to the first empty base in some multiple-inheritance cases, so sizes differ across platforms.

edge_cases.title: Tail-padding reuse makes memcpy of a base subobject dangerous
edge_cases.explanation:
- With the Itanium ABI, a derived class can put members into the tail padding of a non-POD base.
- `struct Base { int x; char c; Base() {} }; struct Der : Base { char d; };`: `sizeof(Der) == 8`, `d` lives at offset 5, inside `Base`'s padding.
- `std::memcpy(static_cast<Base*>(&der), &other_base, sizeof(Base))` overwrites `d`. Copying through `Base`'s assignment operator is safe; raw `memcpy` of a base subobject is not, even for trivially copyable types.
- Remove the user-provided constructor (making `Base` an aggregate/POD) and `sizeof(Der)` becomes 12: the layout depends on whether a base "is POD", a surprising ABI detail.

edge_cases.title: Bit-fields shared between threads
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Flags { unsigned a:4; unsigned b:4; };` with thread 1 writing `a` and thread 2 writing `b` is a data race: both fields are one memory location, and each write is a read-modify-write of the shared byte(s). Updates can be lost.
- TSan reports: "WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race".
- Fix: separate fields (`unsigned char a; unsigned char b;` are distinct memory locations), a zero-width bit-field between them, or one lock/atomic for the whole word.

interview_qa.question: What are `sizeof(A)` and `sizeof(B)` on a typical x86-64 system, and why do they differ?
interview_qa.answer: `sizeof(A)` is 12 and `sizeof(B)` is 8. In `A`, the `int` needs a 4-aligned offset, so 3 padding bytes follow `c`, and 3 bytes of tail padding follow `d` so the size is a multiple of the struct's alignment (4). In `B` the two `char`s share the space after the `int`, leaving only 2 bytes of tail padding.
code_examples:
struct A { char c; int i; char d; };
struct B { int i; char c; char d; };
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Padding depends on member order; `sizeof` includes interior and tail padding.

interview_qa.question: Why does a struct need tail padding, and does a 12-byte struct have to start at an address divisible by 12?
interview_qa.answer: Tail padding makes `sizeof` a multiple of the struct's alignment, because `sizeof` is also the array stride: without it, the members of `arr[1]` would be misaligned. The struct itself only needs an address that is a multiple of its **alignment** (4 for `{char, int, char}`), not of its size.
interview_qa.explanation:
- With `sizeof(A) == 9`, `arr[1]` would start at offset 9 and `arr[1].i` at 13: not 4-aligned.
- With 12: elements at 0, 12, 24, and their `int`s at 4, 16, 28: all aligned.
- `A` can live at 100, 104, 108, ...; 100 is not a multiple of 12 and is perfectly valid.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The struct must start at a multiple of its size" or "of its largest member's size."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `sizeof(T)` is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`; the converse relationship does not exist.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Tail padding exists for arrays; placement depends on alignment, not size.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
Tail padding makes `sizeof` a multiple of the struct's alignment, because `sizeof` is also the array stride: without it, the members of `arr[1]` would be misaligned. The struct itself only needs an address that is a multiple of its **alignment** (4 for `{char, int, char}`), not of its size.

**Explanation:**

- With 12: elements at 0, 12, 24, and their `int`s at 4, 16, 28: all aligned.
- `A` can live at 100, 104, 108, ...; 100 is not a multiple of 12 and is perfectly valid.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `sizeof(T)` is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`; the converse relationship does not exist.

**Key takeaway:** Tail padding exists for arrays; placement depends on alignment, not size.

interview_qa.question: Is "an object's address must be divisible by its size" the correct rule?
interview_qa.answer: No. The rule is "divisible by its alignment requirement" (`alignof(T)`). For `int` on x86-64 both are 4, which makes the wrong rule look right, but they differ for many types: `struct { char c[7]; }` is size 7 alignment 1, `struct { double d; char c; }` is size 16 alignment 8.

- Alignment is always a power of two; size is any multiple of the alignment.
- Scalars: alignment is usually the size on x86-64, but not universally (`long double` is 12 bytes with alignment 4 on 32-bit x86 Linux).
- Precise rules: each member's offset is a multiple of the member's `alignof`; the struct's alignment is the maximum member alignment; `sizeof` is rounded up to that alignment.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The struct's size must be a multiple of its biggest member's size." It is a multiple of its alignment.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: query the numbers with `alignof`/`offsetof` and lock them with `static_assert` instead of reasoning from sizes.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Think `alignof`, not `sizeof`, whenever addresses are involved.

interview_qa.question: Does the compiler reorder members to reduce padding? How do you reduce it, and when should you not?
interview_qa.answer: No. C++ compilers lay out data members in declaration order (guaranteed for members of the same access, and for all members since C++23). You reduce padding yourself, usually by declaring members in decreasing order of alignment. Do not reorder when the layout is an ABI or wire/shared-memory contract, or when grouping hot fields together matters more than a few bytes.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Example: `{char; double; char; int}` is 24 bytes; `{double; int; char; char}` is 16.
- Hot/cold: put the fields the hot path reads on every message in the first cache line, even if that costs padding.
- Tools: `-Wpadded` warns on each inserted padding; `pahole` shows holes in a built binary.
- Lock the result with `static_assert(sizeof(T) == N)` so later edits cannot silently grow it.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The optimizer will rearrange it at -O2." Layout is fixed by the ABI, not by optimisation.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "largest-first" is a heuristic; access pattern and ABI stability come first.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: You own member order; sort by alignment unless ABI or access pattern says otherwise.

interview_qa.question: What does `alignas` do, and can it be used to pack a struct?
interview_qa.answer: `alignas(N)` (C++11) raises the alignment of a variable, data member or class to N (a power of two). On a class it also rounds `sizeof` up to a multiple of N. It can never lower alignment below the natural one, so it cannot pack anything: that needs `#pragma pack` or `__attribute__((packed))`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `struct alignas(64) Line { int x; };` → `alignof` 64, `sizeof` 64.
- `struct S { char c; alignas(16) int x; };` → `x` at offset 16, `sizeof` 32.
- `alignas(1) int x;` is ill-formed: Clang errors, GCC 11 silently ignores it (alignment stays 4).
- `alignas(3)`: error, not a power of two. With several `alignas`, the strictest wins.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`alignas(1)` removes padding."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: typical uses are cache-line separation (`alignas(64)`), SIMD types (`alignas(32)` for AVX), and raw storage (`alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)]`).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `alignas` only strengthens alignment; packing is a different, non-standard tool.

interview_qa.question: What is an over-aligned type, what is `std::max_align_t`, and what does over-alignment do to sizes, arrays, enclosing structs and the stack?
interview_qa.answer: `alignof(std::max_align_t)` (16 on x86-64) is the strictest alignment of any scalar type, the "fundamental" alignment. Its `sizeof` is rounded up to a multiple of the alignment, every array or `std::vector` element and every enclosing struct inherit that alignment, and the compiler realigns stack frames to honour it. Heap allocation of such types needs C++17 aligned `new` (the mechanics are in topic 10 Q8).
code_examples:
max_align_t: 16
Counter: sizeof 64, alignof 64
Holder: sizeof 128, alignof 64
stack aligned: 1, vector aligned: 1
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Over-alignment is contagious: it rounds up `sizeof`, propagates to enclosing types and must be honoured by every allocator; stack and static objects are handled by the compiler.

interview_qa.question: What is a packed struct, and what are the risks of using one?
interview_qa.answer: A packed struct (`#pragma pack(1)` or `__attribute__((packed))`) has no padding: members follow each other byte by byte and the struct's alignment drops to 1. Its members are therefore misaligned, which makes access slower, breaks atomicity and SIMD, can fault on strict-alignment CPUs, and makes pointers or references to members dangerous.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `struct { char c; int i; }` packed: size 5, `i` at offset 1.
- Direct access `p.i` is safe: the compiler knows the member is packed and emits unaligned-safe code.
- `int* q = &p.i;` loses that knowledge. GCC refuses to bind `int&` to an `__attribute__((packed))` member and warns for the pointer (Clang 14 warns for the pointer but accepts the reference); with `#pragma pack` GCC 11 and Clang 14 accepted both silently.
- Arrays of packed structs place most elements at odd addresses.
- Typical legitimate use: describing a wire or file header. Even there, `memcpy`-based parsing into a naturally aligned struct is usually cleaner.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Packing is a free memory optimisation." It trades memory for slower, riskier access.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: reorder members first; pack only when an external byte format forces it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Packing removes padding by creating misaligned members; keep it at the I/O boundary.

interview_qa.question: Is misaligned access undefined behaviour if x86 handles it in hardware? How do you read an `int` at an odd offset of a network buffer?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, it is UB in C++ regardless of the CPU: the compiler may assume every `int*` is 4-aligned (vectorisation, atomics, alias analysis). x86 tolerates plain misaligned loads, but other CPUs fault, SIMD and atomic instructions may fail or lose atomicity, and sanitizers report it. interview_qa.key_takeaway: Never dereference a misaligned pointer; `memcpy` the bytes out.

interview_qa.question: Why is comparing or hashing structs with `memcmp` / raw bytes a bug?
interview_qa.answer: Padding bytes have unspecified values, so two objects with identical members can differ byte-wise: `memcmp` says "different" and a byte hash gives different hashes. interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` (C++17) is true only if equal values always have equal bytes: false for `{char, int, char}` and for `float`, true for `{int, int}`.

- Security angle: writing a padded struct to a socket or file leaks stale stack/heap bytes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "memcmp is just a fast `==`."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `static_assert(std::has_unique_object_representations_v<Key>)` guards a raw-byte hash.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Bytes ≠ value when padding exists; compare and hash members.

interview_qa.question: How can a derived class be smaller than "base size + member size", and why does that make `memcpy` of a base subobject dangerous?

- Use the assignment operator (`static_cast<Base&>(der) = other;`), which copies only `x` and `c`.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: this ABI detail means adding a constructor to a base can change the derived class's size.

interview_qa.question: What is implementation-defined about bit-fields, and why should they not describe a wire format?
interview_qa.answer: The order of bit-fields within their allocation unit, whether a field may straddle units, the unit's size and alignment, and padding between them are all implementation-defined. - ✅ What a strong answer adds: bit-fields are fine for in-memory flags that never leave the process.

interview_qa.question: Two threads each update a different bit-field of the same struct. Is that safe?
interview_qa.answer: No. Adjacent non-zero-width bit-fields form a single memory location, and writing one is a read-modify-write of the shared bytes. interview_qa.explanation:

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Different fields, so no race."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: this is the C++11 memory-model definition of "memory location" in action.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Bit-fields in one run share a memory location; concurrent writes need a single synchronisation point.

interview_qa.question: Does padding exist to keep a struct within a cache line? How do cache lines actually enter layout decisions?
interview_qa.answer: No. Ordinary padding exists only to satisfy member alignment. Cache lines enter layout through explicit choices: keeping structs small and hot fields together so fewer lines are touched, and `alignas(64)` to give variables written by different threads their own line (avoiding false sharing).

- Padding everything to 64 bytes wastes cache; reserve it for a few hot, contended objects.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The compiler pads structs to cache-line size automatically."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the Systems chapter covers false sharing measurements, prefetching and NUMA.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Alignment padding is mandatory and small; cache-line padding is a deliberate, costly choice.

**Explanation:**
- `struct { char c; int i; }` is padded because `int` needs 4-alignment, not because of a 64-byte line.
- False sharing: two threads writing different variables on one 64-byte line bounce the line between cores. `struct alignas(64) Counter { std::atomic<long> v; };` makes each counter occupy a full line (two of them: 128 bytes).
- `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` (C++17, `<new>`) names that distance portably, but libstdc++ only provides it from GCC 12 (with a `-Winterference-size` warning because it depends on `-mtune`); many codebases hard-code 64.
- Padding everything to 64 bytes wastes cache; reserve it for a few hot, contended objects.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The compiler pads structs to cache-line size automatically."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the Systems chapter covers false sharing measurements, prefetching and NUMA.

**Key takeaway:** Alignment padding is mandatory and small; cache-line padding is a deliberate, costly choice.

interview_qa.question: A hot loop sums only the `bid` field of millions of quotes. Should the data be an array of structs or a struct of arrays?
interview_qa.answer: For that loop, a structure of arrays (a contiguous `std::vector<double> bid`) is better: every byte of every cache line loaded is a useful `bid`, and the contiguous doubles vectorise easily. An array of structs wins when the hot code uses most fields of each quote together. The layout should follow the access pattern.
interview_qa.explanation:
- AoS with a 40-byte `Quote`: each 64-byte line holds about 1.6 quotes, of which 8 bytes per quote are used: about 20% useful bytes.
- SoA: 8 bids per line, 100% useful, and SIMD can add 4 doubles at a time (AVX).
- Caveat: a floating-point sum is order-sensitive, so compilers do not reassociate it on their own. GCC 11 `-O3 -mavx2` still adds one double at a time (`vaddsd`); packed `vaddpd` appears with `-ffast-math` (or `-fassociative-math`) or explicit SIMD code; hand-written independent accumulators at least break the serial dependency chain.
- AoS is better for "process one quote completely" because its fields share a line; SoA would touch five separate arrays.
- Hybrids (hot/cold split, AoSoA blocks) exist; the Systems chapter covers them.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "SoA is always faster" or "each AoS element needs its own RAM access" (hardware prefetchers handle regular strides well; the issue is wasted bandwidth and cache capacity).
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: measure with realistic data; the useful-bytes ratio is the first-order effect.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Choose AoS or SoA by which fields the hot loop touches.

interview_qa.question: How do virtual functions and inheritance change an object's layout?
interview_qa.answer: A class with virtual functions gets a hidden vtable pointer (8 bytes, alignment 8 on x86-64), typically at offset 0, so `struct { virtual ~V(); int x; }` is 16 bytes. Base subobjects are laid out first, like leading members. Such a class is no longer standard-layout, so `offsetof` is only conditionally-supported and C-compatible layout assumptions no longer hold.
interview_qa.explanation:
- An `int` alone would be 4 bytes; with a vptr it becomes 8 + 4 + 4 bytes of tail padding.
- Multiple inheritance adds one vptr per polymorphic base subobject; virtual inheritance adds virtual-base offsets.
- `memcpy`/`memset` on polymorphic objects is wrong (they are not trivially copyable; you would overwrite the vptr).
- The object model in depth (vtables, dispatch) is covered in the OOP chapter.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Virtual functions add one pointer per function to every object." One vptr per polymorphic subobject; the table is shared per class.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for millions of small objects, a vptr can double the size; consider type-tagged data or SoA instead.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Polymorphism costs a pointer per object and gives up standard layout.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
24 16 72 8
```

**Explanation:**
- `Trade`: `side`@0, 7 bytes padding, `px`@8, `flag`@16, 7 bytes tail padding → 24 (a multiple of the alignment 8).
- `Trade2`: `px`@0, `side`@8, `flag`@9, 6 bytes tail padding → 16.

- Alignment is the strictest member's: `double` → 8.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
4 8
```
(GCC 11 compiles it and ignores the request; Clang rejects it: "requested alignment is less than minimum alignment of 4 for type 'Msg'". The program is ill-formed.)

**Explanation:**
- `alignas` can only make alignment stricter. A request below the natural alignment of the entity is ill-formed; GCC silently ignores it, Clang reports an error.
- `Msg` keeps alignment 4, `value` stays at offset 4, size 8.
- To remove the padding you need packing (`#pragma pack(push, 1)` → size 5, alignment 1), with all its misalignment consequences, or simply a different member order.
- **Key Concept:** `alignas` raises alignment; it never packs.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: equal: 1, set size: 2
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `Key` has 3 padding bytes after `side`. Their values are unspecified; here `a` has `0xAB` and `b` has zeros there.
- The byte hash includes the padding, so equal keys get different hashes and land in different buckets; `==` is never even consulted. The container's invariant (equal keys have equal hashes) is broken.
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<Key>` is false, which is exactly the warning sign.
- **Key Concept:** Hash and compare members, never the raw bytes of a padded struct.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer:
Data race (undefined behaviour). It prints "done", but TSan reports
"WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race" between the two bit-field writes.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `feed_up` and `seq_lo` are adjacent bit-fields, so together they form one **memory location**. Each assignment is a read-modify-write of the shared byte: one thread can write back a stale copy of the other thread's bits (lost update).
- Separate members (two `unsigned char`s) would be distinct memory locations: no data race.
- Alternatives: a zero-width bit-field `unsigned : 0;` between them (forces a new unit), one mutex for both, or one atomic word updated with `fetch_or`/`fetch_and`.
- **Key Concept:** Different bit-fields are not independent variables for the memory model.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
8 8 12 8
```

**Explanation:**
- Both bases are 8 bytes: `x`@0, `c`@4, 3 bytes of tail padding.
- `D1`: `BaseAgg` is "POD for layout" in the Itanium ABI, so its tail padding is not reused: `d` goes at offset 8 → 12 bytes.
- `D2`: `BaseCtor` is not POD (user-provided constructor), so the ABI is allowed to reuse its tail padding: `d` sits at offset 5 → still 8 bytes.
- Platform-specific: this is the Itanium C++ ABI (GCC/Clang on Linux and macOS); MSVC does not reuse base tail padding this way.
- **Key Concept:** A base's tail padding may hold derived members, and whether it does can depend on seemingly unrelated details.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
sizeof(Der)=8 d before: X
x=1 d after: 0
```

**Explanation:**
- `Der::d` lives at offset 5, inside `Base`'s tail padding (Q5). `memcpy` of `sizeof(Base)` = 8 bytes copies `src`'s padding byte (zero, because `src` has static storage) over `d`.
- The standard forbids exactly this: the trivially-copyable `memcpy` guarantee does not cover potentially-overlapping subobjects (base classes, `[[no_unique_address]]` members). The program has undefined behaviour; this output is what GCC produced.
- Fix: `static_cast<Base&>(der) = src;` copies only `x` and `c`.
- **Key Concept:** Never `memcpy` into a base-class subobject; use its assignment operator.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
128 64 64 68 128
```

**Explanation:**
- `head`@0, `tail` must be 64-aligned → offset 64; `buf` follows at 68.
- The struct's alignment is 64, so 84 bytes of data round up to 128.
- `std::vector` places elements `sizeof(Queue)` apart and, since C++17, uses aligned allocation so every element is 64-aligned.
- `head` and `tail` are on different cache lines: producer and consumer no longer invalidate each other's line (false sharing avoided). `buf` shares `tail`'s line; in a real ring buffer the data would also be separated.
- **Key Concept:** `alignas(64)` on members separates hot variables, at the cost of a larger struct.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: cannot bind packed field 'h.Header::length' to 'uint32_t&' {aka 'unsigned int&'}
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `length` sits at offset 1. A `std::uint32_t&` promises a 4-aligned object, which a packed member cannot guarantee, so GCC refuses (taking `&h.length` only warns with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`).
- With `#pragma pack(push, 1)` instead of the attribute, GCC 11 compiled the same code silently: the danger is still there, only the diagnostic is missing.
- Compiler-specific: Clang 14 compiles this exact program (attribute version) without any diagnostic, even with `-Wall -Wextra`, and prints 101. Only GCC rejects it.
- Fix: copy out, modify, copy back: `auto n = h.length; bump(n); h.length = n;`.
- **Key Concept:** References and pointers to packed members are misaligned pointers in disguise.
practice_tasks.key_concept: References and pointers to packed members are misaligned pointers in disguise.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
not active -1 1
```

**Explanation:**
- A signed 1-bit field can only hold 0 and -1 (two's complement, guaranteed since C++20). Storing 1 sets the single bit, which reads back as -1, so `f.active == 1` is false.
- GCC even says so with `-Wextra`: "comparison is always false due to limited range of data type [-Wtype-limits]".
- `level` has 2 bits; 5 is `101` in binary, the low two bits `01` are kept → 1. (Assigning the constant `5` directly would trigger GCC's `-Woverflow` warning; through a variable there is no warning.)
- Fix: use `unsigned active : 1;` or `bool active : 1;` for flags.
- **Key Concept:** Bit-fields silently truncate, and 1-bit signed fields are a classic boolean bug.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: cannot bind bit-field 'p.Pair::a' to 'unsigned int&'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::swap` takes its arguments by non-const reference. A bit-field is not addressable (it may start in the middle of a byte), so no `unsigned&` can refer to it.
- The same applies to `&p.a`, `std::cin >> p.a`, and any API taking `T&`.
- Fix: swap through temporaries.
- **Key Concept:** Bit-fields are not objects with addresses; generic code expecting references does not accept them.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
7/1 8 16 10
```

**Explanation:**
- `Sym7` is 7 bytes with alignment 1: its alignment comes from its member `char`, not from its size.
- `WithChar`: 7 + 1 = 8, alignment 1, no padding.
- `WithDouble`: `s`@0-6, padding to 8, `px`@8 → 16.
- `WithShort`: `c`@0, `s`@1-7 (alignment 1, so no padding before it), `qty` needs 2-alignment → offset 8, size 10 (a multiple of 2).
- Reasoning with "divisible by size" would wrongly place `s` at offset 7 or pad `Sym7` to 8.
- **Key Concept:** Offsets follow each member's `alignof`; an array of chars has alignment 1 whatever its size.

quick_reference.content:
#### Layout rules
| Rule | Detail |
|---|---|
| Member offset | Multiple of the member's `alignof` |
| Struct alignment | Max of member/base alignments (or `alignas`) |
| `sizeof(struct)` | Rounded up to a multiple of its alignment (tail padding) |
| Array stride | `sizeof(T)`; `alignof(T[N]) == alignof(T)` |
| Member order | Declaration order, never reordered by the compiler |
| Empty class | `sizeof` 1; 0 as base (EBO) or `[[no_unique_address]]` member |
| Over-aligned | `alignof > alignof(max_align_t)` (16 on x86-64); heap support since C++17 |

#### Sizes on x86-64 Linux (GCC/Clang)
| Struct | sizeof | alignof |
|---|---|---|
| `{char; int; char}` | 12 | 4 |
| `{int; char; char}` | 8 | 4 |
| `{char; double; char; int}` | 24 | 8 |
| `{double; int; char; char}` | 16 | 8 |
| `{char; alignas(16) int}` | 32 | 16 |
| `alignas(64) {int}` | 64 | 64 |
| `{virtual dtor; int}` | 16 | 8 |
| packed `{char; int}` | 5 | 1 |
| `{unsigned a:3, b:5, c:24}` | 4 | 4 |

#### Tools
| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Lock a layout | `static_assert(sizeof/alignof/offsetof ...)` |
| Find holes | `-Wpadded`, `pahole` |
| Safe unaligned read | `std::memcpy`, `std::bit_cast` |
| Align inside a buffer | `std::align` |
| Byte-wise compare/hash valid? | `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` |
| Detect misaligned access | `-fsanitize=alignment` (part of `undefined`) |
| Cache-line padding | `alignas(64)` / `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` (GCC 12+) |

#### Interview one-liners
- "Members go at multiples of their alignment; the struct's size is rounded to a multiple of its alignment so arrays stay aligned."
- "Alignment is not size: `alignof`, not `sizeof`, decides valid addresses."
- "Sort members by decreasing alignment to cut padding, unless hot/cold grouping or ABI says otherwise."
- "`alignas` only raises alignment; packing lowers it and makes members misaligned."
- "Misaligned access is UB even if x86 tolerates it; copy bytes out with `memcpy`."
- "Padding bytes are unspecified: never `memcmp` or hash a padded struct."
- "Empty members cost a byte plus padding; use a base or `[[no_unique_address]]`."
- "Adjacent bit-fields are one memory location: two threads writing different fields is a data race."
- "`alignas(64)` separates hot variables written by different threads: false sharing is a layout bug."
